forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 29 to 29. A hold, and I want to be explicit that this is a considered hold rather than a failure to look. I checked every one of yesterday's six stated update triggers and none of them fired cleanly in either direction. No lab announced AGI. No named senior researcher - as distinct from a CEO - stated that AGI has been achieved. The two things that did move today are a headline fall in the closest real-money instrument that dissolves on inspection into a thin-volume quote artefact, and a modest firming in the Polymarket Astra ladder that partly reverses yesterday's slip. They roughly cancel.

The Kalshi print is the item that would otherwise have driven a move, so I want to handle it carefully rather than take the headline. Kalshi's KXOAIAGI series now displays 'Before 2030' at 36 per cent, marked down 7.2 on the day from yesterday's 43.2, with 'Before 2028' at 18 per cent (down 3 from 21) and 'Before 2027' at 6 per cent (up 1 from 5). Taken at face value that is a seven-point fall in the single most relevant liquid market and would justify two points off my central. It is not what happened. Series volume today reads $894,366 against $894,281 yesterday - roughly eighty-five dollars of turnover in twenty-four hours on a market that has done nearly nine hundred thousand dollars lifetime. And the quoted spread tells the same story from the other side: Yes 43.4c / No 64c today implies a bid of 36c and an ask of 43.4c, against yesterday's Yes 43c / No 62.7c implying a bid of 37.3c and an ask of 43c. The ask actually rose four tenths of a cent. What moved is the bid, by 1.3c, and the displayed 'chance' appears to have flipped from tracking the upper end of a very wide spread to tracking the lower end. A 7.4-cent bid-ask on a 2030-dated contract is enormous, and the midpoint - about 39.7 per cent - is essentially unchanged from yesterday's midpoint. I therefore take -1pp for genuine bid-side softening across two rungs rather than the -2pp the headline implies, and I flag that anyone reading the Kalshi tape today without opening the order book will draw a much more dramatic conclusion than the data support.

Against that, the Polymarket Astra ladder firmed. Yesterday's rungs were 39 per cent for 15 September, 76 per cent for 30 September and 89 per cent for 31 October. Today they read 41.5 per cent, 79 per cent and 89 per cent, with 31 August still deep in the low teens or below. That is a two-to-three point recovery on the near rungs, unwinding a good part of the slippage I scored at -0.5pp yesterday. It does not tell me OpenAI is closer to a declaration; it tells me traders have marginally reduced their estimate of how long the 7 August cybersecurity hold persists. Still, the Astra ladder is my cleanest available proxy for near-term frontier delivery at the lab most likely to declare, and it moved the right way. +0.5pp.

The genuinely substantive capability item on my tape is one I had not previously counted, and having gone back to the primary source I am giving it weight even though it is five days old. Anthropic published on 20 August a study in which Claude autonomously ran a de novo protein binder design campaign, with the designs manufactured and wet-lab tested by two independent third parties. Adaptyv Bio built all 1,320 designs in a cell-free system; Twist Bioscience independently evaluated 1,260 of them as antibody fusions in human cells in under three weeks. Claude produced working binders against 14 of 15 targets, with per-design success rates of 22 to 35 per cent depending on setup against an industry baseline Anthropic puts at 10 to 15 per cent, high-affinity binders against at least six targets, and binders matching or exceeding the best reported affinity against at least four. Against RBX1 the Mythos preview hit 40 per cent where human entrants in an Adaptyv competition managed 3.7 per cent, and Claude's top design beat the winning human entry. Forbes wrote it up on 23 August. This is the strongest third-party wet-lab-validated evidence I have seen of a model doing autonomous scientific work end to end, and autonomous science is one of the two mechanisms - the other being AI accelerating AI research, where Prime Intellect's NanoGPT Speedrun Frontier landed yesterday - that could plausibly underwrite a defensible AGI declaration inside forty months. +1pp.

But here is the disciplining observation, and it is why I am not moving up. That result has been public since 20 August. The Goodheart Labs combined forecast, which I pulled fresh this morning and which is explicitly timestamped 'as of August 25, 2026', still reads a median of 2031 with an 80 per cent band of 2027 to 2043 - identical to yesterday and to a fortnight ago. Metaculus Q5121 still carries a January 2033 median with roughly 25 per cent by 2029. Kalshi has fallen, not risen, over the same window. A genuinely timeline-compressing result should show up in at least one of these. That it has not is evidence that the aggregate treats narrow-domain autonomous science, however impressive, as orthogonal to the general-capability threshold this question asks about. I am not going to be the only forecaster repricing on it.

One modest negative I did add. The Google situation is now clearly documented rather than inferred: Google has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026, Gemini 4 only began pre-training on 21 July 2026 with no announced release date, Koray Kavukcuoglu took over on roughly 5-6 August with Hassabis moving to chairman and Alphabet Chief Scientist, and Inc. counted eight prominent researchers departing in two months. One of the three institutions with the standing to make a credible AGI declaration is materially behind and mid-reorganisation. That thins the field of potential declarers through 2027 at least. -0.75pp.

What I checked and found nothing on. ARC Prize has issued no ruling on NVIDIA's AVO claim and no statement at all; the Verified Leaderboard is unchanged and NVIDIA's own framing now explicitly cautions that the 100.00 RHAE public-set figure and ARC's ~30 per cent for Opus 5 'should not be interpreted as a direct measurement' because they used different agent systems and evaluation setups - which is close to conceding the point I made yesterday. No news on OpenAI's Preparedness Framework rewrite since Axios on 18 August. No Anthropic public S-1; the June 1 confidential draft still stands with an October Nasdaq target, and CNBC's 21 August reporting on expected risk factors mentions AI backlash, model misuse, regulatory uncertainty and compute constraints, with nothing on AGI framing either way. The AGI Global Summit running in Portland is an academic cross-disciplinary event producing a report 6-8 months out; it involves economists, philosophers and lawyers, not frontier lab research staff, and cannot plausibly generate a resolving statement. Nvidia infrastructure news continued to compound - Groq 3 LPX in full production on 24 August, the Cloverleaf partnership on 21 August, the $105bn Ohio financing for OpenAI capacity phasing in from 2028 - but these are multi-year-lag inputs and I score them at most +0.5pp.

Net: ups of about +2.0, downs of about -2.25. That rounds to zero. Holding 29, band unchanged at 17-45.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is still no historical frequency of AGI declarations to draw on. The event has occurred zero times in the seventy years since the 1956 Dartmouth coinage, so the outside view has to be assembled from standing forecast aggregates and structurally analogous reference classes rather than an event count. That remains the single largest limitation on this forecast and the reason the interval stays as wide as 17-45.

Reference class one, my primary anchor: standing aggregate forecasts on AGI timing. I re-pulled the Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard this morning and it now carries an explicit 'as of August 25, 2026' timestamp on a combined median arrival of 2031 with an 80 per cent confidence band running 2027 to 2043. That is unchanged from yesterday, from a week ago and from a fortnight ago. It aggregates five instruments: Metaculus 'weakly general AI' (Q3479), Metaculus 'general AI' (Q5121), Metaculus's long adversarial Turing test question (Q11861), Manifold's 'AGI When? [High Quality Turing Test]' distribution, and Kalshi's Turing-test-before-2030 market. A 2031 median with that right skew implies roughly a quarter to a third of probability mass falling before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121's community median sits near January 2033 with roughly 25 per cent by 2029; its 'weakly general AI' sibling, which drops the robotics condition, carries a far earlier median around mid-2028, and the gap between the two is itself informative about how much of the disagreement is definitional rather than empirical. These are large-n, long-running, incentive-checked estimates and I let them set the centre of gravity in the high twenties to low thirties. The instruments are correlated - overlapping populations, overlapping information - so the effective sample is smaller than the headline forecaster counts suggest. Worth noting that the Manifold aggregate underlying the Goodheart dashboard now puts the adversarial-Turing-test year at 2034 across 1,100-plus contributors, which is later than most of the ladder markets and pulls the combined band's right tail out.

Reference class two: the specific declaration markets. Kalshi's KXOAIAGI series is the closest liquid instrument, but it asks a strictly narrower question than mine (OpenAI specifically, announcement only) and simultaneously a laxer one (no researcher-consensus alternative, and arguably a lower bar for what counts as 'announce'). Today it displays 'Before 2030' at 36 per cent, down 7.2, on a quoted Yes 43.4c / No 64c - a bid of 36c against an ask of 43.4c, so a 7.4-cent spread and a midpoint near 39.7 per cent, essentially unchanged from yesterday's midpoint. Series volume is $894,366, up about eighty-five dollars on the day. The near rungs read 18 per cent for Before 2028 and 6 per cent for Before 2027. I read the fair value of this instrument as somewhere in the high thirties to low forties, and I note it also carries a persistent long-dated-market bias: capital tied up until 2030 demands a discount, which pushes fair value above the traded price. Manifold's parallel ladder - roughly 3 per cent for 2027, 15 per cent for 2028, 31 per cent for 2029, 38 per cent for 2030, 45 per cent for 2031, 52 for 2032, 55 for 2033 - is play-money and lightly capitalised but monotone, internally coherent, and brackets the aggregate view. I read this cluster as consistent with something in the 30s for a broad AGI-arrival question and rather lower for a strict institutional-declaration question.

Reference class three, and the one that keeps me below the raw market numbers: the frequency with which prominent declarations have already occurred without resolving anything. Jensen Huang told Lex Fridman in late March 2026 that AGI has already been achieved, and Fortune's write-up on 30 March documented researchers immediately disputing it. Sam Altman told Forbes the company had 'basically built AGI, or very close to it,' then walked it back as a 'spiritual' rather than literal statement requiring 'a lot of medium-sized breakthroughs.' Dario Amodei at Davos in January 2026 put it at one to three years. Demis Hassabis has repeatedly said roughly fifty-fifty by 2030 and explicitly not via systems built like today's. Sequoia has published that 'AGI is here, now.' Satya Nadella says the industry is nowhere close. Yann LeCun says LLMs will never get there. None of these resolved this question, none moved Kalshi's 2027 rung above about 6 cents, and none produced three named senior researchers - as distinct from CEOs and investors - asserting achievement within a short window. This is the crux, and it is why I hold a substantial gap between 'a system plausibly deserving the label exists' and 'a credible lab announces, or three leading researchers state, that it has been achieved.' The base rate of loose CEO-and-VC AGI talk is high and rising; the observed conversion rate into a resolving social event remains zero out of at least five.

Reference class four: technology-declaration analogues where a field must collectively agree a threshold was crossed - room-temperature superconductivity claims, quantum supremacy, self-driving 'Level 5'. The pattern is that contested definitions plus commercial incentives produce claims that are individually loud and collectively non-resolving for years. Quantum supremacy took roughly three years from Google's 2019 claim to broad but still incomplete acceptance. This class fits well on structure and poorly on stakes: AGI has vastly larger commercial and regulatory consequences, which cuts both ways - more incentive to claim, far more liability for claiming wrongly, particularly with both OpenAI and Anthropic now inside IPO windows. The ARC Prize verification apparatus is the institutionalised version of exactly this dynamic, and NVIDIA's own updated framing of AVO - conceding that its 100.00 public-set figure and ARC's ~30 per cent for the same underlying model 'should not be interpreted as a direct measurement' because the agent systems and evaluation setups differ - is a live demonstration that the machinery works to blunt claims rather than convert them.

A fifth consideration I now weight explicitly: the field's own governance behaviour. The 'Pacing the Frontier' letter of 28 July 2026 drew over 1,260 signatures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and Thinky staff, including Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, asking Washington to build the technical and policy tools to deliberately slow frontier development if recursive self-improvement arrives; both Anthropic and OpenAI endorsed it corporately within a day. This is genuinely double-edged. It is the strongest available signal that senior insiders think automated AI R&D is plausible within a few years - which supports the upper part of my band. It is also a coordinated pre-commitment to institutional caution, and organisations that have publicly endorsed a slowdown mechanism are markedly less likely to issue a triumphal 'we have achieved AGI' press release.

Integrating: the outside view puts me around 28-32 for a broad arrival question over the remaining roughly forty months. Inside-view adjustments are close to a wash. Upward: the harness and scaffolding channel is visibly productive and cheap, the AI-doing-AI-research channel now has third-party open evidence, autonomous science has wet-lab third-party validation, and compute supply and financing keep compounding. Downward: safety-gated release regimes are real and costly, enterprise willingness to pay for the frontier looks capped, measured productivity effects remain near zero, Google is mid-reorganisation and has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026, and imminent public listings raise the liability cost of a declaration. I sit at 29, a few points below the Kalshi midpoint, because the resolution bar is a social event and the observed conversion rate from capability claim to resolving declaration remains zero.
factors_up: Anthropic's third-party wet-lab-validated autonomous protein design result, published 20 Aug and written up by Forbes on 23 Aug (+1.5pp). Claude autonomously ran a de novo binder campaign; Adaptyv Bio built all 1,320 designs and Twist Bioscience independently tested 1,260 as antibody fusions in human cells in under three weeks, producing working binders against 14 of 15 targets at 22-35% per-design success versus a 10-15% industry baseline, high-affinity binders against six-plus targets, and a 40% hit rate on RBX1 where human competition entrants managed 3.7%. Autonomous end-to-end science with independent physical validation is one of the few mechanisms that could underwrite a defensible AGI declaration inside forty months.

Polymarket's Astra ladder firmed on 25 Aug, partly unwinding yesterday's slip (+0.5pp). The 15 September rung moved to 41.5% from 39%, the 30 September rung to 79% from 76%, with 31 October holding at 89%. Traders have marginally shortened their estimate of how long OpenAI's 7 August cybersecurity hold persists, which is my cleanest available proxy for near-term frontier delivery at the lab most likely to declare.

Compute capital and power supply kept compounding through 24-25 Aug (+0.5pp). Nvidia put the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator into full production on 24 August, partnered with data-centre developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure on 21 August, and is backing up to $105bn of financing for OpenAI's Ohio campus covering an initial 4.25GW with an option on a further 3.75GW phasing in from 2028, alongside the $500bn third-party financing platform with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman and KKR. These are multi-year-lag inputs and I do not let them move much.

The 'three or more leading AI researchers' pathway remains structurally softer than an institutional declaration and requires no lab to ship anything (+2pp). Huang in March 2026, Altman in Forbes, Amodei at Davos, Hassabis at fifty-fifty by 2030 and Sequoia's published 'AGI is here, now' show that senior-figure declarations already occur at meaningful frequency; the resolver only needs three of them to be researchers rather than executives and to land in a short window.

The 'Pacing the Frontier' letter is an insider signal that recursive self-improvement is considered live (+1pp). Over 1,260 staff across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and Thinky signed on 28 July 2026, including Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, on the explicit premise that AI systems 'may soon be able to automate their own research and development.' That is a large, named, cross-lab body of senior technical opinion putting non-trivial weight on a fast takeoff inside my window.
factors_down: Kalshi's KXOAIAGI ladder softened on the bid side across two rungs (-1pp). 'Before 2030' displays 36% against 43.2% yesterday and 'Before 2028' 18% against 21%, though the quoted Yes 43.4c / No 64c implies a 36-43.4c spread with a midpoint near 39.7% that is essentially flat, and series volume rose only from $894,281 to $894,366 - about eighty-five dollars of turnover. I score the genuine bid-side softening, not the headline seven-point fall, which is largely a display artefact on a near-zero-volume day.

Google, one of only three institutions with standing to make a credible AGI declaration, is materially behind and mid-reorganisation (-1pp). It has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026, Gemini 4 only entered pre-training on 21 July 2026 with no announced release date, Koray Kavukcuoglu replaced Demis Hassabis as head of Google DeepMind in early August with Hassabis moving to chairman and Alphabet Chief Scientist, and Inc. counted eight prominent researchers leaving in two months. That thins the field of plausible declarers through 2027.

The aggregate forecasts have not moved despite a fortnight of strong capability results (-1.5pp). Goodheart Labs' combined estimate is explicitly timestamped 'as of August 25, 2026' at a 2031 median with an 80% band of 2027-2043, identical to a fortnight ago; Metaculus Q5121 still shows a January 2033 median with roughly 25% by 2029; Manifold's adversarial-Turing-test distribution across 1,100-plus contributors sits at 2034. Neither the Anthropic protein result nor the Prime Intellect autonomous-research result nor the AVO harness claim has compressed any of them.

Safety-gated release regimes remain a real and unresolved brake (-1.5pp). OpenAI's Astra has been on hold since 7 August after preliminary evaluations could not rule out a 'critical' cybersecurity capability - defined as developing functional zero-days in hardened real-world systems without human intervention - with isolated testing environments, sandboxed execution, restricted network and tool access and additional monitoring required before deployment, and the Preparedness Framework rewrite unresolved since Axios reported it on 18 August.

The industry has publicly pre-committed to institutional caution, which cuts against triumphal declaration (-1pp). Anthropic and OpenAI both corporately endorsed 'Pacing the Frontier' within a day of the 28 July letter, formally backing a mechanism to deliberately slow frontier development. Organisations on that record, both inside IPO windows - Anthropic's confidential S-1 filed 1 June targeting an October Nasdaq listing, OpenAI saying it will be public by 2027 - face heavy liability for an AGI claim they cannot defend.

Five-plus senior-figure AGI-adjacent declarations have produced zero resolutions (-3pp). Altman has explicitly retracted his own to a 'spiritual' rather than literal claim requiring 'a lot of medium-sized breakthroughs'; Fortune documented researchers disputing Huang's March 2026 claim within days; NVIDIA has now itself conceded that its AVO 100.00 figure 'should not be interpreted as a direct measurement' against ARC's leaderboard. The observed conversion rate from loud capability claim to resolving social declaration remains zero.
key_uncertainties: Whether the resolver counts a scaffold-plus-model system, or a domain-specific autonomous result like the protein binder campaign, as 'AGI achieved' at all, or requires general capability intrinsic to a released model. NVIDIA's AVO, Inherent's Faraday and Anthropic's Claude Science are exactly the ambiguous cases and no resolver guidance exists.

How 'credible lab' and 'leading AI researchers' bind in practice, given that at least five senior-figure declarations have already occurred without resolving this question, one has been publicly walked back by its author, and the three-researcher pathway has no defined window or seniority threshold.

Whether the Kalshi display convention change is noise or the leading edge of genuine repricing. The bid-ask on the 2030 rung is 7.4 cents wide and daily turnover is negligible, so the instrument I lean on most heavily may be carrying far less information than its headline volume suggests.

Whether OpenAI's Astra hold, the roughly 20% monitoring compute overhead and the Preparedness Framework rewrite become a durable structural brake through 2029, or resolve into a delay of weeks - Polymarket currently splits the difference at 79% by 30 September.

Whether the 'Pacing the Frontier' consensus, corporately endorsed by both Anthropic and OpenAI, makes an institutional AGI declaration materially less likely, or is compatible with one framed as a safety warning rather than a product claim.

Whether Google returns to frontier contention inside the window. Gemini 4 began pre-training on 21 July 2026 and its performance will determine whether there are three plausible declarers in 2027-2029 or effectively two.
update_triggers: Revise UP if three or more named senior research staff - not CEOs, not investors - at OpenAI, Anthropic or Google DeepMind state within a short window that AGI has been achieved, or any lab issues an institutional statement using the phrase 'we have achieved AGI'

Revise UP if ARC Prize places any system above 80% on the ARC-AGI-3 Semi-Private or Private sets on the Verified Leaderboard (still reading Opus 5 30.2%, GPT-5.6 Sol 7.8%, Opus 4.8 1.5%), or if NVIDIA open-sources AVO and submits it under the Kaggle verification process

Revise UP if the Goodheart Labs combined median moves inside 2030, or if Metaculus Q5121's implied probability by 2029 rises above 35%, either of which would be the first aggregate compression in a fortnight
Revise UP if Kalshi KXOAIAGI 'Before 2030' trades above 55 with a bid-ask inside 3 cents and series volume rising by more than $20,000 in a week, rather than the current ~$85/day on a 7.4-cent spread

Revise DOWN if Anthropic's public S-1 (October Nasdaq target) contains risk-factor language explicitly disclaiming near-term AGI, or if OpenAI's rewritten Preparedness Framework imposes a formal capability ceiling or external sign-off plausibly binding through 2029

Revise DOWN if the Polymarket Astra ladder slips past 31 October (currently 89%), if Gemini 4 slips to 2027 or launches materially below GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5, or if further enterprise-spend data confirms a durable ceiling on willingness to pay for frontier capability

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 11 to 11. Third consecutive hold, and this one is the emptiest of the three in terms of genuinely new information. None of yesterday's nine update triggers fired. I checked each in turn. FTI's Q3 print is not due until late October, so the trigger on a second consecutive quarter of Economic Consulting headcount decline cannot fire yet. The Challenger August report and the BLS August employment situation both land on or around 4 September, so neither the AI-cuts-spreading-outside-Technology trigger nor the CES6054160001 three-month-decline trigger has anything new to test against; the most recent Challenger release remains the July report published 6 August, whose headline the firm itself titles 'Layoffs Fall, Hiring Picks Up; AI Leads For Fifth Straight Month.' No listed comparator in the narrow niche — CRA, Huron, Cornerstone, NERA, Compass Lexecon, Brattle, Analysis Group — has disclosed anything since CRA's 7 August call. No new quantified estimate of AI-caused consultancy decline exceeding 15% from a 2024 base has appeared from Source Global Research, IBISWorld, the FT or the ONS. Searches on consultancy.uk and consulting.us surfaced nothing dated 23, 24 or 25 August 2026 beyond routine transaction and appointment items — AlixPartners acquiring Artium (an agentic-AI software consultancy in Los Angeles), Andersen Group agreeing to acquire UK Andersen LLP and SPR Consulting, and Milliman naming Jim Fulton chief executive from October 2026. Note the direction of the AlixPartners deal: a consultancy buying AI capability to sell, which is the demand-amplifier reading, not the substitution reading.

Four items are new to my log, and they roughly cancel.

First, and the most substantive: the BLS Monthly Labor Review's 2024–34 industry and occupational employment projections article, published in 2026, projects 9.4% employment growth for Management, Scientific and Technical Consulting Services over 2024–34, with IT consulting demand explicitly named as a driver because firms need help implementing AI tools. I should have had this earlier and did not. It matters because it is the official US statistical agency, forecasting the exact NAICS 5416 aggregate that a broad-reading resolver would use, over a decade that fully contains the resolution window, and it projects growth of roughly plus 0.9% a year against the minus 9.0% a year the question requires. It is not a market-research house with a commercial interest in a growing market, which is the objection available against IBISWorld and Mordor. Weight: minus 0.4pp.

Second, cutting the other way: S&P Global's 'The AI and labor landscape 2026' special report, based on its PMI special survey, has revised its net employment assessment. A prior vintage found a neutral-to-slightly-positive net employment impact from AI adoption; the 2026 report finds a negative global net impact over the past twelve months at minus 5 points and a marginal further decline forecast for 2026 at minus 2 points. Larger firms increasingly anticipate net negative impacts, and the report flags rapid maturation of investment in AI agents as an accelerant. That is a credible forecaster moving in the direction the question needs. But the roles it names as shrinking are administration and office support, translation, manufacturing, production and customer service — the same clerical-and-routine cluster that has dominated every displacement dataset I have looked at — and consulting is not among them. Direction up, sector composition down. Weight: plus 0.3pp.

Third, an extension of the value-repricing thread I logged yesterday off the Forbes piece. A Financial-News item puts Accenture at more than 57% of market value lost over twelve months and Capgemini at nearly 40%, while noting in the same breath that most firms are still posting decent sales growth. That is a much larger drawdown than the single-session minus 18% on 18 June 2026 I had recorded. I am weighting it lightly for two reasons. The question's resolution criteria specify 'revenue or employment,' not market capitalisation, so a resolver almost certainly cannot use equity value even though the question stem says 'value.' And the same source explicitly separates the price move from the revenue trajectory, which is the Jemma Green point restated. Weight: plus 0.3pp.

Fourth, a capability datapoint rather than a market one: xAI's Grok Bot, introduced 11 August 2026, described as an agent that uses computers and software tools, works across applications, learns workflows and completes tasks end to end. Agentic computer use that owns a workflow rather than assisting a task is the specific capability shape that would make client-side insourcing of economic analysis cheap. This is exactly the 2029-30 tail risk I said I could not bound with any reference class, and it is now slightly less hypothetical. But it is a fortnight-old product announcement with no deployment evidence in professional services, and I have watched several such announcements pass through this series without moving any consulting metric. Weight: plus 0.3pp.

One hygiene note, and it is the same failure mode I flagged on 24 August with the phantom PwC story. Today's searches returned a cluster of confident-sounding claims that McKinsey is cutting 3,000 to 4,000 roles, roughly 10% of headcount, explicitly because AI substitutes for junior analyst work. If true that would be a material up-move. It is not new and it is not well sourced. The claim appears only on SEO content farms — metaintro, finalroundai, outsourceaccelerator — and traces back to the November 2025 reduction of roughly 200 technology and support staff plus Bob Sternfels's comment that more non-client-role reductions would follow over two years, with the larger number appearing to be extrapolation dressed as reporting. No FT, WSJ, Bloomberg or Reuters version exists in the results. I am not logging it. Two further items in the same category: the Accenture '11,000' and '22,000' cut figures belong to the $865m restructuring announced in Q4 FY2025 (September 2025) and are already in my prior; and KPMG's roughly 10% cut to US audit partners, about 100 partners, is dated 23 April 2026 and concerns audit, not consulting, though Thomas Mackenzie's line that within two to three years there will be 'next to no human beings' performing routine audit testing is a genuinely striking piece of insider testimony about the adjacent profession.

Netting: plus 0.9pp of new up-weight against minus 0.4pp of down-weight, on items I would classify as weak evidence individually and mutually offsetting collectively. That is well inside the rounding band and I hold at 11. Band stays 6 to 19: the BLS projection argues faintly for trimming the top, the S&P Global revision and the Grok Bot launch argue faintly for keeping it, and I am not going to churn the interval on a day this thin. The next genuinely informative dates are unchanged: 4 September for Challenger August and the BLS August employment situation, and late October for FTI's Q3 and CRA's Q3 prints.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is unchanged and remains a poor fit, which is still the single dominant fact in this forecast. The class is: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with that loss attributed primarily to one identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Membership is sparse and every candidate fails at least one of the three conjoined criteria.

US travel agency employment fell roughly 40-50%, clearing the magnitude bar, but over roughly fifteen years from 1998 and with two distinct causes — online booking platforms and the abolition of airline commissions in 1995-2002. A resolver applying a primarily-attributed-to-one-technology test would very likely reject it. Contract document review contracted sharply once predictive coding and technology-assisted review became defensible in US discovery, but the affected population was contract attorneys and staffing agencies rather than a profession, and legal services revenue grew throughout. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third with desktop publishing as a clean single cause, but over more than a decade and against a physical craft with no advisory, judgement or relationship component. Bank tellers declined slowly and partially, with ATM deployment coinciding with two decades of branch expansion. Stock-photography contributors and switchboard operators are mismatched on either timescale or the professional-judgement dimension. Across the broader pool of technology-disruption episodes visible enough to be forecastable in advance, the modal outcome over five to six years is task recomposition with flat-to-rising sector employment, not a one-third contraction. Base rates for a named professional sector losing a third of value inside six years, technology-caused or otherwise, sit in the low single digits per episode.

The outside view therefore anchors at roughly 5-8% for the magnitude leg alone on a generic professional-services sector over 2024-2030. Two adjustments pull in opposite directions.

Upward: the inside view has real content. The task profile of economic and management consulting — literature synthesis, data cleaning, econometric scaffolding, slide production, first-draft expert reports — maps unusually well onto current frontier-model capability in a way travel booking never mapped onto anything in 1995. Adoption is fast: Thomson Reuters has organisational genAI use in professional services at 40%, up from 22% a year earlier, and its 2026 AI in Professional Services report now finds the binding constraint is a guidance gap rather than a capability gap. The leverage pyramid that makes consulting profitable is exactly the layer under pressure, and the Big Four graduate intake data (KPMG down 29% from 1,399 to 942, Deloitte down about 18%, EY down 11%, PwC UK down 6%, PwC US planning a 32% campus cut by 2028) shows firms acting on that belief with their own money. Agentic tooling that owns whole workflows rather than assisting single tasks — xAI's Grok Bot on 11 August 2026 is the latest instance — is the specific capability shape that would make client-side insourcing cheap, and S&P Global's 2026 labour report flags rapid maturation of AI-agent investment as an accelerant while revising its net global employment impact from neutral-to-positive to minus 5 points over the past year. Four years and four months of runway remain. That argues for lifting the magnitude leg to perhaps 12-18% under a narrow reading isolating the expert-witness and competition-economics niche, and 4-6% under the broad BLS management, scientific and technical consulting aggregate.

Downward: the observed data run hard against the magnitude leg, and today's addition strengthens that side. BLS series CES6054160001 stood at 1,886,600 in July 2026, with June's 1,888,100 the highest reading in the series' 36-year history, against a 2024 average of 1,860,500; professional and business services added 14,600 jobs in July 2026. The maximum drawdown in the entire series is 6.0%, in the February-April 2020 shock, recovered within a year. The question needs roughly minus 9.0% a year sustained for 53 consecutive months — nothing in the series history is within a factor of five of that. The new item is that the BLS itself, in the Monthly Labor Review's 2024-34 industry and occupational employment projections published in 2026, forecasts 9.4% employment growth for exactly this industry over exactly this window, naming AI-implementation demand as a driver rather than a threat. That is the official statistical agency, with no commercial interest in the answer, projecting roughly plus 0.9% a year where the question needs minus 9.0%. It sits alongside IBISWorld's July 2026 Scientific and Economic Consulting report at $65.6 billion, up 2.6% in 2026 on a 4.1% five-year CAGR with 16.4% margins, and Mordor's management consulting market growing 4.70% a year to $471.39 billion in 2031.

Within the narrow niche the listed comparators remain visibly dispersed rather than uniformly expanding: CRA at $210.8 million and plus 12.8% with headcount up 3.3%, against FTI Economic Consulting at $188.8 million and minus 1.5% with headcount down 2.1% and margin at 4.7%. But the spread runs from minus 2% to plus 13%, and the question asks about minus 33%. Dispersion of that width is normal cyclical noise in a case-flow business, not the leading edge of a collapse.

Integrating: the magnitude leg sits at roughly 13-16% on a resolver-weighted blend of narrow and broad readings, and the attribution leg at roughly 0.65-0.72 conditional on a decline of that size occurring. Conditional on a genuine one-third collapse, AI would almost certainly become the consensus explanation and two credible analyses saying so would be easy to find — but not certain. FTI's own disclosure remains the live worked example of the attribution problem: the one economic-consulting business that is actually contracting attributes it to antitrust case flow and is simultaneously litigating against a breakaway competitor for poaching its experts. The product lands at 8.5-11.5%. I sit at 11, at the top of that range, because the conjunction arithmetic is deliberately conservative and the 2029-30 tail — a capability step making client-side insourcing trivial — is genuinely hard to bound and is represented in no reference class I have.
factors_up: FTI Consulting 8-K of 30 July 2026 (+3pp): the Economic Consulting segment is the only one of five with falling billable headcount, 970 at 30 June 2026 against 991 a year earlier (-2.1%), while Corporate Finance rose 7.8% and Forensic and Litigation Consulting 3.0%; segment revenue -1.5% to $188.8m (-2.1% ex-FX), utilisation down from 64% to 61%, Adjusted Segment EBITDA margin down from 7.4% to 4.7% (H1: 0.8% versus 7.7%). This is the most literally on-point series available for the phrase 'economic consultancy' and every operating metric deteriorated year on year. Q3 is due late October and is the single most informative scheduled release in this forecast.

Structural fee-model erosion (+3pp): roughly a quarter of McKinsey's global fees now outcome-based, BCG projecting AI-tied revenue rising from ~20% of 2024 revenue to ~40% in 2026, Lilli running 500,000+ prompts a month with consultants citing up to 30% time savings. This is the clearest route to a value decline without a headcount collapse, and it is the leg of the question least visible in employment statistics. Hybridhero's 2026 margin analysis frames sustained client fee pressure and AI-changed delivery as jointly compressing margins even where revenue holds.

Challenger July 2026 report of 6 August (+3pp): AI led all stated job-cut reasons for a fifth consecutive month at 10,970 cuts (33% of July's total), taking 2026 year-to-date AI-cited cuts to 112,713 (~24% of all cuts) and cumulative since 2023 to 184,538. Financial-News puts Accenture down more than 57% of market value over twelve months and Capgemini down nearly 40%, extending the single-session -18% on 18 June 2026 and Gartner's ~-21% day in February. Equity value is not the resolution metric, but a sustained repricing of this size is at minimum a market forecast of revenue trouble.

Agentic capability step plus a forecaster revision (+2pp): xAI's Grok Bot, introduced 11 August 2026, is described as an agent that uses computers and software tools, works across applications, learns workflows and completes tasks end to end — the capability shape that would make client-side insourcing of economic analysis cheap. S&P Global's 'AI and labor landscape 2026' has revised its net global employment impact from neutral-to-slightly-positive to -5 points over the past twelve months with a further -2 forecast for 2026, citing rapid maturation of AI-agent investment, with larger firms increasingly anticipating net negative effects.
factors_down: BLS now projects growth in exactly this industry over exactly this window (-5pp): the Monthly Labor Review's 2024-34 industry and occupational employment projections article, published 2026, forecasts 9.4% employment growth for Management, Scientific and Technical Consulting Services, explicitly naming demand for help implementing AI tools as a driver. That is roughly +0.9% a year from an official statistical agency with no commercial interest in the answer, against the -9.0% a year for 53 consecutive months the question requires. It is the strongest single disconfirming datapoint in the file because it is immune to the commercial-interest objection available against IBISWorld and Mordor.

The one contracting economic-consulting business names a non-AI cause (-4pp): FTI attributes the Economic Consulting decline to 'lower demand for non-merger and acquisition-related antitrust and international arbitration services', while the $6.6m of Extraordinary Litigation-Related Expenses relate to FTI vs. Orszag et al., where the Maryland court in May 2026 allowed a third amended complaint adding competitor Econic Partners LLC and former employee Dr Mark Israel on trade-secrets claims. Senior-expert defection, not automation; Compass Lexecon was still adding academic affiliates in May 2026, and FTI firm-wide billable headcount was still up 3.2% with 270+ graduates due in Q3.

Sector revenue forecasts uniformly positive through the resolution window (-3pp): IBISWorld July 2026 puts US scientific and economic consulting at $65.6bn, up 2.6% in 2026 on a 4.1% five-year CAGR with 16.4% margins; Mordor has management consulting at $374.67bn in 2026 rising to $471.39bn by 2031 on a 4.70% CAGR; MCA projects UK growth of 5.7% in 2026 and 7.4% in 2027 with AI services the single largest growth driver; Source Global Research has tech consulting passing $400bn with 81% of buyers intending to increase reliance on consultants. AlixPartners' acquisition of agentic-AI consultancy Artium this week is a live instance of firms buying AI capability to resell rather than being displaced by it.

Attribution bar looks harder to clear, not easier (-3pp): a February 2026 survey of ~6,000 C-suite executives across four countries found 80%+ reporting no AI impact on productivity or employment; SHRM's 2026 Automation/AI survey finds client preferences the single most common non-technical barrier to displacement, present in 62.7% of jobs with any such barrier — a barrier that binds especially hard in expert testimony, where the client is a court; the 95%-of-pilots-show-no-profit finding was still being repeated in Forbes on 21 August 2026; Challenger warns tracking will get 'more opaque' as regulation arrives.
key_uncertainties: Whether FTI's Economic Consulting contraction is the leading edge of something or pure idiosyncrasy — one quarter of -1.5% revenue and -2.1% headcount, with the firm itself blaming antitrust case flow while suing a breakaway competitor over expert defections, is exactly what a cyclical trough plus a talent shock looks like; CRA's +12.8% and +3.3% headcount in the same quarter and niche is the strongest argument that it is idiosyncratic, and late October gives a clean second reading on both

How the resolver scopes 'economic consultancy': the narrow expert-witness and competition-economics niche (CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Compass Lexecon, Analysis Group, Brattle, Bates White, BRG) could diverge enormously by 2030 from the BLS management, scientific and technical consulting aggregate that the agency itself now projects growing 9.4% to 2034, and the two readings imply magnitude-leg probabilities differing by a factor of three

Whether the seniority-pyramid restructuring visible in postings and graduate-intake data ever converts into an aggregate headcount decline, or simply reallocates work upward while total employment holds at record levels — McKinsey's simultaneous global back-office cuts and 12% North American junior hiring increase remains the sharpest live instance, and the poorly sourced 3,000-4,000-cut claims circulating on content farms are a reminder that this particular story attracts fabrication

Whether the attribution requirement is satisfiable in practice, given that any 2026-30 contraction will have overlapping macro, regulatory, offshoring and AI causes, that firms hedge AI language in redundancy statements (KPMG's April 2026 UK cuts named no AI; FTI's segment decline names antitrust demand; KPMG's US audit partner cut cited 'scale of audit work' before AI), and that Challenger expects tracking to become more opaque

Whether fee compression from outcome-based pricing shows up as a revenue decline or is absorbed by volume: if delivery time halves and firms take on more engagements, value holds while hours collapse, and the question's 'revenue or employment' framing may catch neither — FTI's Economic Consulting average billable rate rose from $593 to $633 even as utilisation fell, which is the opposite of a price-collapse signature

Whether agentic tools that own end-to-end workflows (Grok Bot, 11 August 2026, and successors) cross the threshold where corporate legal and economics teams insource competition and damages analysis — this is the 2029-30 tail I cannot bound with any reference class, and SHRM's finding that client preference is the dominant non-technical barrier suggests court and regulator acceptance of AI-produced expert analysis is the binding constraint rather than capability

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 51 to 52. As with yesterday, this is not a polling move, and I want to establish that before anything else. BritPolls' complete 2026 archive, refetched this morning, still lists twenty polls with the most recent GB fieldwork ending 19 August: Find Out Now, Lab 23.0, Ref 23.0, Con 18.0, Grn 14.0, LD 11.0, n=2,287. Behind it sit Survation 18/8 (Lab 26, Ref 26, n=2,013), YouGov 16-17/8 (Lab 22, Ref 24, n=2,441), Deltapoll 17/8 (Lab 29, Ref 27, n=2,017) and More in Common 17/8 (Lab 27, Ref 25, n=2,055). PollCheck's seven-poll moving average is still stamped 21 August and still reads Lab 26.0, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6, Grn 10.6, LD 10.3 - identical to the last three days. BritPolls' live ticker reads Ref 25.0, Lab 25.4, Con 19.6, Grn 10.8, LD 10.4, also unchanged. Six days have now elapsed since the last completed fieldwork. Parliament remains in recess. There is no new national voting intention to report and I am not going to invent a trend from a static average.

What has changed is my ledger rather than the world. Three items surfaced today that were not carried in yesterday's factor list, and two of them are mildly favourable to Labour.

The first and largest is that Nigel Farage is under live parliamentary standards jeopardy, and the clock restarted this month. The Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards has been investigating him since May over a GBP 5m gift received before his 2024 election and not declared on entering the Commons; the published rectification record establishes seventeen separate breaches of Rule 5 of the Code for failure to register interests inside the 28-day window. Farage resigned the Clacton seat on 7 July 2026 - The Sunday Times having reported undeclared benefits paid for by a convicted fraudster - which automatically suspended the inquiry, and he re-contested and won the by-election on 13 August with 62 per cent, on a ballot Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats and Restore Britain all declined to fight. The commissioner reopened the case the day after. ITV's 14 August explainer sets out the escalation path: a finding of breach goes to the Committee on Standards, which can recommend anything from an apology to suspension, and a suspension exceeding ten sitting days triggers a recall petition in Clacton. I do not think this threatens Reform's seat count - Farage would very likely hold a 62 per cent constituency at any re-run - but it does put the leader of the party whose entire polling proposition is anti-establishment authenticity into a months-long drip of funding-scandal coverage running straight through the autumn. It also gives a mechanical reading to something I already had in the ledger: Farage's YouGov net favourability of -44 (23 per cent favourable against 67 per cent unfavourable, 55 per cent 'very unfavourable'), down seventeen points from -27 in May 2025. Some of that deterioration is presumably this. I weight the item at +2pp and no more, because it is a fortnight old, because the polls have already had time to absorb it, and because Reform's vote has proved repeatedly indifferent to Farage's personal ratings.

The second item cuts against my own largest DOWN factor. I have been carrying the 28 October Budget as a dated, quantified honeymoon-killer, and I still do. But Healey is not walking into it cold. VAT is being removed from household electricity bills from 1 October, three and a half weeks before the Budget, and Burnham has signalled a 20 per cent business rates reduction for pubs, clubs and music venues plus a higher rates threshold for small independent hospitality and retail. Healey has framed the Budget itself as an event that 'moves money and power out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain'. That is a deliberate sequencing: a visible cost-of-living giveaway lands first, the fiscal pain lands second, and the whole thing is wrapped in devolution framing that plays to Burnham's single strongest personal asset. It does not make the GBP 24bn NIESR-identified shortfall go away, and the 2024 manifesto lock on income tax, NI and VAT is still the fiscal cul-de-sac every commentator names. But it materially reduces the probability that the Budget is an unambiguous disaster, and I was not pricing that mitigation at all. Call it +2pp against the Budget factor, which I trim from -4pp to -3pp.

The third item is a small shift on the Ladbrokes timing market, and it is the one place I have to be honest about reading a single bookmaker's rounding as signal. Yesterday's ledger recorded 2029-or-later at 10/11 (52.6 per cent raw). The board I pulled today prices 2029 or later at 1/1, with 2028 at 7/2, 2027 at 9/4 and 2026 at 16/1. Normalising that book of 108.9 per cent gives roughly 46 per cent for 2029 or later - so slightly over half the implied mass now sits on an election before 2029. That is one notch of movement and could be nothing. But my central estimate contains a five-to-eight point discount purely for three-plus years of decay risk in a shallow 26 per cent coalition, and if the expected horizon shortens, that discount should shrink a little. Worth about +1pp.

Against those three, one item goes the other way, and it is the third consecutive failure of my pre-registered market-corroboration trigger. I required a live dated price from Betfair Exchange, Smarkets or a prediction market quoting Labour most-seats at or inside 11/8. Today I got something better than another blank: ElectionOdds.com, which states plainly that it aggregates the public APIs of Polymarket and Kalshi twice daily, lists no UK most-seats market at all. Its live board carries only 'Nigel Farage out as Reform UK leader in 2026?' (No 81 per cent, Yes 20 per cent, $226,468 traded) and a plainly broken 'Next UK Prime Minister in 2026?' listing four different names all at 46 per cent. Its narrative text is dated June 2026 and still describes Keir Starmer as prime minister. So the conclusion is not that I failed to find the corroborating market; it is that the liquid prediction markets do not price this question. My entire market anchor rests on one bookmaker's board, on a page whose copy has read 'Updated at: 21 Jul 2026' for three days running, even though the betslip prices themselves have held at Labour 11/8, Reform 11/5, Con 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1. That persistence is real evidence the prices are live; the absence of any second venue means I should not weight them more heavily than the quarter-weight I already give. Call it -1pp, and I am now retiring this trigger in its current form because it has failed three times for a structural reason rather than a contingent one.

On the seat models there is nothing. Electoral Calculus's prediction page is still the 28 July refresh - Lab 244 seats on 23.9 per cent, Ref 127 on 23.4, Con 132 on 19.7, LD 70, SNP 44, Grn 10 - with P(Labour largest) 58 per cent, Reform 25, Conservative 16, and a 90 per cent Labour seat range of 88-357. My trigger requiring a refresh above 58 per cent has not fired. The 20 August council by-elections resolved as a small Labour edge and a small Reform reverse: across four wards Labour averaged 30.1 per cent to Reform's 29.6, with Reform down one net, and Penistone East returning two of three seats to Labour. That is consistent with the councillor-attrition story I already carry and adds nothing new. Netting up: two modest new positives, one very small positive, one small negative, and no polling at all. One point.
forecasts.base_rate:
The obvious reference class - incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election - gives roughly 65-70 per cent for the incumbent still being largest party, about thirteen of nineteen defences since 1945. I continue to treat it as badly mis-specified and use it only as a loose upper anchor. Every case in that class comes from a two-and-a-half party system where the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent. No governing party in it ever entered mid-term polling at 22-29 per cent with four rivals at or above 8 per cent. The current PollCheck seven-poll average has five parties between 10.3 and 26.0. Sample nineteen, fit poor, no more than a fifth of my weight.

A second class - governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then contested the following election - fits better and flatters less, though it splits sharply. Major, Brown, May, Johnson, Sunak: two of five were largest party at the next contest, a base rate near 40 per cent on a sample of five, contaminated because mid-term leader changes are usually a symptom of an already-losing position. Burnham differs measurably. The change has been followed by a genuine recovery: from 16-20 per cent in YouGov's series across Starmer's last six months to 21-24 since; from a ten-point Reform lead in January 2026 to a one-point Labour lead on the current aggregate; and to a personal rating YouGov calls the best for any prime minister on its ten-year tracker since Boris Johnson in May 2020. Post-Major and post-Brown produced no such recovery. Post-Johnson under Sunak produced a partial one that decayed. So this class is informative about the risk of decay, not about the starting level - and Richard Rose's 30 July judgement that the Burnham bounce 'will fade rapidly' is the mainstream expert prior on precisely that decay.

The third and most load-bearing consideration is structural rather than historical: the seat-vote translation. Electoral Calculus's current poll-of-polls, updated 28 July on 13,321 respondents polled 7-27 July, returns Lab 244 seats on 23.9 per cent against Reform 127 on 23.4 - roughly ten Labour MPs per point of national vote against just over five for Reform. Its 23-30 June MRP for PLMR (n=5,545) turned Lab 22 = Ref 22 into Lab 217, Con 151, Ref 127, LD 72, Grn 30, SNP 28. Convergent's 25-30 July MRP returns Lab 245 v Ref 174 v Con 99 on Lab 26.1 v Ref 23.2. Even BritPolls' cruder average model has Lab around 280 v Ref around 100. In every one of these Labour is largest from vote-share parity or a low single-digit lead, because Labour's shallow 33.7 per cent 2024 coalition is geographically efficient while the right-of-centre vote splits three ways between Reform, the Conservatives and Restore Britain. Electoral Calculus's tactical-voting work adds a further Reform penalty, with over a third of Labour voters willing to vote Conservative to keep Reform out.

I continue to discount that mechanism from where I had it a week ago. Its magnitude depends on how large Restore Britain really is, and direct measurement disagrees with the modelling assumption. PollCheck's dedicated tracker puts Restore Britain at 3.0 per cent on its seven-poll average - Survation 2.0 (20/8), YouGov 4.0 (19/8), Ipsos 4.0 (9/8) - against the 7 per cent Electoral Calculus's June MRP attributed to it. Only three of eleven active pollsters prompt for the party by name, so unprompted Restore Britain support may be sitting inside Reform's numbers rather than outside them. Pulling the other way is the only hard electoral test: Makerfield, 18 June 2026, where Rebecca Shepherd took 6.8 per cent (3,111 votes), third of six and ahead of the Conservatives on 2.2 per cent, in a seat where Reform were 2024 runners-up. A real ballot beats a prompt-list artefact, but one ballot is one ballot. I treat the right-split component as worth about +8pp rather than +10pp, with wide error.

Integration. I take the structural seat evidence as implying roughly 55-58 per cent for Labour largest on an election-now basis, which is where Electoral Calculus itself sits at 58 per cent. I discount four to seven points for the horizon - slightly less than the five to eight I applied yesterday, because the Ladbrokes timing book has shifted a notch toward a pre-2029 contest and now implies only about 46 per cent for 2029-or-later once normalised. Three years of decay in a shallow 26 per cent coalition remains a serious risk; the 28 October Budget under a chancellor 66 per cent of the public cannot place, against a NIESR-identified GBP 24bn hole, is a canonical honeymoon-killer, though the 1 October VAT cut on household electricity bills is a deliberate pre-emptive sweetener; and Reform has years to build the organisation it currently lacks. I then blend in the live bookmaker consensus at about a quarter weight. Normalising the Ladbrokes most-seats book of 105.7 per cent gives Labour roughly 40 per cent, Reform 31, Conservatives 22 - and its majority book gives No Overall Majority 4/7, Labour majority 4/1, Reform and Conservative majorities 7/1 each, so the market agrees a hung parliament is the modal outcome and disagrees with Electoral Calculus mainly about who leads it. I allow that favourite-longshot bias on multi-outcome political markets typically understates the favourite, but I hold the weight low rather than high precisely because no second venue prices this question. That lands in the low fifties. I stay above 50 because the seat arithmetic is a real, quantified and repeatedly replicated asymmetry rather than a tie. The 36-64 interval reflects Electoral Calculus's own 90 per cent seat ranges of 88-357 for Labour and 53-289 for Reform: the structural uncertainty over this horizon is enormous, and the gap between a 58 per cent model and a 40 per cent market is itself an honest statement of how little anyone knows.

forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 84 to 84. No declaration-shaped event on 24-25 August, and the day's up-signals and down-signals are close enough in magnitude that the disciplined answer is to hold. I checked the AI Weekly live tape for Tuesday 25 August (179 tracked stories this week, 113 tracked entities) and the top five stories are Nvidia's Groq 3 LPX inference rack entering full production with Nebius as first customer, Taiwan indicting nine people over 130 smuggled Nvidia B300 servers, the Alabama Attorney General subpoenaing OpenAI, a 825m euro Dutch DPA fine against Uber over automated driver deactivations, and General Intuition's valuation nearly tripling to 6bn dollars pre-money in eight weeks. The standing precedent on the resolution-event limb is unchanged: Huang's March 2026 'we've achieved AGI' to Lex Fridman, Altman's late-July singularity framing, Goertzel's AGI-26 nine-to-twelve-months remark. Hold on limb one and limb two.

The single largest genuinely new item is one I had not logged, and it is nine days old rather than twenty-four hours: the AI Futures Project published its Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update on 16 August (Lifland, Kokotajlo, Halstead; page last modified 18 August). It matters because it is the most rigorously documented timeline model in the field and it now anchors Automated Coder three ways rather than one. The headline: timelines 'haven't changed much (they got slightly shorter)'. Daniel's all-things-considered AC median moves from May 2028 in April to Nov 2027 in August, with TED-AI (their AGI analogue: at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks) at a Nov 2028 median and ASI at Mar 2029. Eli's AC median moves from Jul 2030 to Jan 2030, TED-AI Jul 2032, ASI Jul 2033. Brendan, forecasting for the first time, puts AC at Jan 2029 and TED-AI at Apr 2031. Every one of the three TED-AI medians falls inside 2035. Most directly usable for this question: Brendan writes that 'the model's 70% on AC by Jan 2030 and nearly 90% by Jan 2035 feels too confident, so I reduce these to 60% and 80%'. That is an explicit 80 per cent by January 2035 for a milestone weaker than AGI, from the most conservative of the three authors, and it sits almost exactly on my central.

But the same document contains the discount that stops this being a move up. In the appendix the authors state plainly, and for the first time: 'from now on our forecasts are for what will happen conditional on things going as fast as is technically feasible' - i.e. conditional on no government intervention to slow things down. They note they had previously implied they were adjusting for non-technical slowdowns and in practice had not. This question is unconditional. Given the direction of the governance tape - OpenAI reversing itself on 22 August to ask California to strengthen SB 53, the EU AI Act general-purpose obligations live since 2 August, Anthropic's 11 August EU-compliance watermarking rollout, and now a state Attorney General subpoena - the conditioning is not a formality. Their second discount is the AI 2027 grading: reality is running at 'roughly 70-90% the speed of AI 2027'. So the anchor arrives bullish and self-discounted, and lands close to neutral for me. On the crux uncertainty I flagged yesterday - whether the messy-task gap is a harness problem or an architectural one - the 24 August tape adds a third data point on the harness side. A 70-author paper, 'Apodex 1.1: Scaling Agentic Intelligence for Complex Work' (arXiv 2608.23283), was the top Hugging Face Papers trend of the day with 88 upvotes. Its two claimed scaling axes are 'Environment Scaling' (expanding executable code environments) and 'Agentic Coordination Scaling' (parallel task delegation across a shared execution harness), and it claims leading results on finance, scientific research, maths, coding and search using smaller models than frontier systems, with a 35B 'Mini' variant positioned for local deployment. It is not independent replication - all three are self-reported by interested parties, and AVO's 100.00 RHAE is explicitly public-set only, with ARC Prize's own site showing AVO does not score 100 on the semi-private games - but the direction is consistent and it is why the messy-task factor stays at -4pp rather than reverting to -6pp.

The hardware tape cuts both ways and roughly cancels. On the supportive side, Nvidia's Groq 3 LPX - the dedicated inference accelerator out of the 20bn dollar Groq acqui-hire - entered full production on 24 August, slotting into Vera Rubin at up to 256 accelerators per rack, with Artificial Analysis clocking 3,400 output tokens per second on Gemma 4 31B at 100K context. Silicon is now being co-designed for long-horizon agentic loops, which is the exact bottleneck AVO-style harnesses hit. Broadcom is in talks for more than 60bn dollars, potentially 100bn, via an SPV to lease custom chips to Anthropic and others, targeting 20 GW of AI capacity by 2028, and Anthropic hired Amir Salek, founder of Google's TPU programme. Morgan has DRAM up more than 400 per cent from start-2024 to end-2026, with 2026 at +245 per cent year on year and another +36 per cent in 2027; memory is about 30 per cent of hyperscaler capex in 2026 heading for 36 per cent in 2027; Nvidia's 15 per cent-plus price rise on Rubin and Blackwell systems bites from early-2027 shipments. Outside-view anchors are literally unchanged. The Goodheart Labs dashboard, fetched live today, reads a combined median of 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2043, stamped 'as of August 24, 2026' - identical to yesterday's read. Kalshi's KXAGICO-COMP rules text still matches this question's first limb almost exactly, requiring an explicit statement that a company has 'achieved, attained, reached, or developed' AGI and excluding 'AGI-like', 'AGI-level', 'near-AGI' and 'toward AGI'. Netting: a strong but explicitly no-slowdown-conditioned new timeline anchor, a third method-over-scale paper, and agent-optimised silicon shipping, against an economy-scale productivity null result, a state Attorney General subpoena, and a memory crunch now forecast to persist to 2029. forecasts.base_rate:
There is no frequency base rate here. AGI has never been developed, so the event class has zero members and no historical frequency can be computed. The only usable outside view is the distribution of published forecasts on near-identical questions, treated as a reference class of forecaster distributions rather than of events. I track six anchors and weight them by how closely their resolution criteria match this question's, which is a rhetorical, announcement-shaped bar rather than a capability bar.

First, the cross-platform aggregate. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, which combines Metaculus 3479, Metaculus 5121, the Metaculus adversarial Turing question, Manifold's high-quality-Turing-test market and Kalshi, and is funded by Jaan Tallinn, reads live today at a combined median of 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2043, stamped 'as of August 24, 2026'. Fitting a right-skewed distribution through 10th percentile 2027, median 2031, 90th percentile 2043 puts roughly 69 to 75 per cent of mass before 1 January 2035. The asymmetry is the important feature: four years separate the 10th from the 50th percentile but twelve separate the 50th from the 90th, so cumulative probability rises steeply through the late 2020s then flattens into a long tail that 2035 sits inside but not deep inside. This is my strict-definition anchor and it has now been static for two consecutive days.

Second, Metaculus's flagship strict question 5121. The community median for the first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced stands at January 2033, from a pool of more than 1,800 forecasters. That definition requires broad robotic as well as cognitive capability, the strictest common bar in the field, which mechanically pushes the median later than any announcement-based criterion. A January 2033 median implies roughly 60 to 68 per cent of mass before 2035, and this question's bar is materially easier. The weakly-general companion question 3479 carries a June 2028 median. The direction matters: from 2025 into 2026 the Metaculus community pushed timelines out rather than in, which is the main reason I do not simply take the market-implied high-80s.

Third, the announcement-shaped markets, which match this question's first limb most closely. Kalshi's KXAGICO-COMP series, 'Will any company achieve AGI before [date]?', resolves Yes only if a company explicitly states it has 'achieved, attained, reached, or developed' AGI; statements describing 'AGI-like', 'AGI-level', 'near-AGI' or 'toward AGI' systems expressly do not qualify. That rules text is close to this question's first limb. The ladder I have logged reads roughly 41 per cent before January 2028, 42 per cent before April 2028 and 59 per cent before July 2028, on about 92,000 dollars of volume with a wide 47c/60c spread on the 2028 tranche, with previously logged tranches near 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031. On naive hazard continuation those extrapolate to the mid-to-high 80s by 2035. This is my most bullish anchor and also the one most exposed to the chip-and-memory saturation argument, since it assumes the post-2030 hazard rate matches the pre-2030 rate. Thin volume and wide spreads argue for treating the levels as indicative.

Fourth, the sceptical real-money end. Polymarket gives OpenAI about 9 per cent for AGI by 2027; Kalshi's OpenAI-specific line reads about 14 per cent before 1 December 2026 and 18 per cent before 1 January 2027. Money is consistently more cautious than rhetoric, and the near-dated markets have the cleanest resolution criteria, which is a reason to respect them even though they say little directly about 2035.

Fifth, the rigorously elicited expert panels, still the strongest brake. LEAP wave 8, fielded 20 April to 11 May 2026, puts the superforecaster median AGI year at 2047 with only 80 per cent before 2100, and economists at 60 per cent before 2100. Wave 9, fielded 19 May to 10 June 2026 with 194 experts, 53 superforecasters and 612 members of the public, covers catastrophe and governance risk rather than timelines, so the 2047 median stands unrefreshed. If it is right, mass before 2035 is well under 30 per cent. I do not weight it heavily, because its definition is stricter still and superforecaster panels have been systematically late on AI capability questions since 2021, but the spread between LEAP's 2047 and Kalshi's implied high-80s by 2035 is wider than my entire confidence interval and is the honest reason the interval stays wide.

Sixth, and upgraded in weight today, the explicit structural models. The AI Futures Project's Q2.5 update of 16 August 2026 gives Automated Coder medians of November 2027 (Kokotajlo), January 2030 (Lifland) and January 2029 (Halstead), and TED-AI - their AGI analogue, at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks - at November 2028, July 2032 and April 2031 respectively. All three fall inside 2035. Halstead states the model's raw output is 'nearly 90%' on AC by January 2035 and hand-adjusts to 80 per cent. Critically, the authors now state that all their forecasts are conditional on 'things going as fast as is technically feasible', with no adjustment for government-imposed slowdown, and their own AI 2027 grading has reality running at 70-90 per cent of scenario pace. Treated unconditionally, these numbers should be shaded down by whatever probability one assigns to a material non-technical brake over nine years. Alongside them, FutureSearch's tracker (12 April 2026) records every updater between January and April 2026 moving earlier; Wiblin's 6 August retrospective reports his own timelines shortening by about a year; Christiano's March 2026 note puts us at the 90th percentile of his 2019 and 2021 timelines. Frontier Timelines' 18 August weekly aggregate central estimates read AGI 2028, full RSI 2030, ASI 2031. Lab-leader rhetoric sits earlier still: Altman placing AGI inside the current presidential term, Amodei's powerful AI by 2027, Hassabis at Davos in January 2026 at roughly 50 per cent by end of decade while noting one or two more breakthroughs in reasoning and world models are needed. Sequoia's Grady and Huang published '2026: This is AGI' arguing long-horizon agents are functionally AGI already, which is term inflation in exactly the direction limb two rewards.

Weighting the strict-definition anchors at roughly 70 per cent and the announcement-shaped anchors at roughly 85-88, then adding for the second resolution limb - three leading researchers stating AGI is achieved, a bar Huang, Altman, Goertzel and the Sequoia framing arguably already stress - the outside view lands in the low-to-mid 80s. Subtracting for the possibility that no serious lab ever uses the word, which the 27 April 2026 removal of the OpenAI-Microsoft AGI clause made concrete, brings it to 84.
