forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 7 to 7. No update trigger fired in the last 24 hours, and the two genuinely new pieces of evidence I found today - one adverse, one reassuring - are close enough in weight that the honest action is to hold both the central estimate and the 4-12 interval I widened yesterday.

Start with the trigger checklist. Taiwan's MND daily tally for 24 August was 2 PLA aircraft sorties, 7 PLAN vessels and 2 official ships (ANI, 24 Aug 2026, 08:48 IST); the 23 August reading was zero aircraft with 7 PLAN vessels and 7 official ships, and 22 August was 3 sorties, 8 PLAN vessels and 7 official ships with all three sorties crossing the median line into the northern and southwestern ADIZ. Nothing in the last 72 hours breaks the pattern I described yesterday: an air component pinned at or near its floor, a naval component flat at 6-9 hulls, and a coastguard component oscillating between 2 and 7. There is still no Fujian MSA navigation warning anywhere in August, still no named exercise since Justice Mission 2025 - now eight full months, the longest gap since 2022 - and still no boarding of a Taiwan-bound merchant vessel under Coast Guard Order No. 3. The mobilisation indicators specified in trigger four (reserve call-ups, RO-RO requisition, ammunition prepositioning, hospital surge orders) remain absent. Polymarket's end-2026 invasion market is unchanged at 4 percent on roughly 40 million dollars of volume, with the 30 September market at 1 percent; the same market was near 30 percent in late 2025, so the market's own trajectory this year has been downward.

The new adverse fact concerns the carrier gap, and it is a partial correction to my reasoning yesterday. I discounted the western Pacific carrier vacancy on the grounds that Theodore Roosevelt had finished COMPTUEX and RIMPAC and would most likely fill the Pacific. The War Zone's 17 August carrier location survey says something different: Roosevelt is still pierside in San Diego, and the assessment is that when she sails she will 'likely just pass through the region on its way to the Middle East,' with a September deployment probably intended to relieve Abraham Lincoln in CENTCOM. If that is right, the western Pacific gap does not close in September - it persists, and Bryan Clark's arithmetic (11-carrier fleet, two continuous deployments, two carriers held for Iran, therefore months each year at zero Pacific presence) starts to look less like a projection and more like a description. Compounding this, I had not been pricing the arms-sale pause: the Washington Post reported on 23 May that the 14 billion dollar Taiwan package announced in January was put on hold after the Beijing summit, and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said explicitly it was paused 'in order to make sure we have the munitions we need for Epic Fury.' Lai was still publicly asking for approval 'as soon as possible' on 18 June (France 24), and I can find no evidence it has been released. Three months of a frozen 14 billion dollar package, on top of the pre-existing delivery backlog, is a real subtraction from Taiwan's 2027-29 capability curve - which is where most of this question's probability mass sits. A third, smaller item runs the same way: on 11-12 August a PLAN vessel conducted the first-ever joint navigation exercise with a foreign navy - Indonesia's KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai - in waters east of Taiwan, with Global Times quoting an expert saying it demonstrated 'China's sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan island.' Taiwan's MOFA called it a military provocation. Recruiting a third country into a jurisdictional claim east of Taiwan is precisely the normalisation groundwork a quarantine would need.

The new reassuring fact is analytic rather than operational, and it strengthens the down side more than I expected. I found the Taiwan Security Monitor's four-author study (Reed, Walberg, Connell, O'Connor, Schar School, 7 March 2026) of the February-March stand-down. It is an independent second look at the same episode Drew Thompson wrote about on 6 March, and it works systematically through five hypotheses - Two Sessions and Spring Festival seasonality, purge-induced incapacity, pre-summit 'best behaviour', Middle East fuel conservation, and pre-campaign preparation - and rejects the last three. On incapacity: PLAN activity around Taiwan stayed consistent and the PLA and CCG remained active at the Senkakus and Scarborough Shoal, with the Southern Theater Command publicising a combined early-warning, ASW, fighter and bomber patrol on 28 February. On fuel: China's strategic petroleum reserve runs to hundreds of millions of barrels and is still being expanded, and a fuel constraint would have suppressed activity everywhere rather than only near Taiwan. On invasion prep: a theatre-level operation would generate naval redeployments, unusual airbase activity and logistical movement that open-source and satellite monitoring reliably detect, and none appeared. Their conclusion is that the lull reflects 'routine variability inherent in sustained military operations' and cyclical calibration of pressure rather than a change of strategy. Two independent expert teams have now examined a 2026 PLA lull for pre-campaign signatures and found none. That does not make the current seven-month structural halving benign, but it does further weaken the tail scenario in which quiet is the tell.

Two smaller down items. First, the CCP's fifth plenum has been called for October 2026 and, unusually, is set to focus on 'strict party governance' and internal discipline rather than the five-year plan (Vision Times, 5 Aug; Storm Media). With the 21st Party Congress in 2027, that is another political set-piece absorbing leadership bandwidth in the near window, alongside the September Washington summit and November APEC in Shenzhen. Second, I need to soften yesterday's political-warfare factor: the ISW-AEI update of 18 August records that Taiwan's opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan finally passed the 2026 general budget after a near year-long delay and approved the Cabinet's full 2 billion dollar drone budget. The larger special act for uncrewed systems - which GTI's Emerson Tsui puts at NT$335bn citing MND, against the NT$210bn figure in earlier reporting - does remain deadlocked, so the factor survives, but at reduced weight.

One item is genuinely two-sided. Tsui's 12 August GTI brief documents that Taiwan's Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee ran its first tabletop exercise on 'high-intensity maritime coercion' on 25 June, with eleven ministries, modelling a phased CCG escalation: harassment, then a requirement that vessels entering and leaving Taiwanese ports report through China's International Trade Single Window, then inspection, then boarding, then detention and seizure. Taipei is now war-gaming the exact ladder I think is modal. But Tsui's own analytic point cuts against YES resolution: a declared quarantine is Beijing's preferred option precisely because it is law-enforcement-framed, reversible and unlikely to draw third-party intervention, whereas a blockade is a state-versus-state act that may. The instrument Beijing is building is the one least likely to be described by two major agencies as a blockade.

Net: an adverse structural revision on US posture, an equally weighty analytic reinforcement of the restraint reading, and no threshold crossed. Hold at 7, interval unchanged at 4-12.
forecasts.base_rate:
Four reference classes bear on this question, and I weight the first and fourth most heavily.

The broad class is major-power initiation of an opposed amphibious assault, or a sustained naval blockade of a defended and populated territory, since 1945. The candidate set is thin: Inchon in 1950 against a state already at war, Suez in 1956, the Cuban quarantine of 1962 which was a partial interdiction lasting under a month, the Falklands in 1982 which was a British counter-invasion of a lightly garrisoned archipelago, the Iran-Iraq tanker war of 1984-88, Russia's Black Sea grain interdiction from 2022, and the US naval blockade of Iran begun on 13 April 2026 and still running at more than four months, with CENTCOM having redirected 70 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 as of late August. Roughly seven episodes across eighty years, against a denominator of perhaps twenty to thirty dyads at any time possessing both capability and a claimed casus belli. That implies an annualised hazard per capable dyad of roughly 0.5 to 2 percent. Applied to the 3.35 years from today to 1 January 2030, that yields about 2 to 7 percent. The Iran case is a live addition to the class and marginally raises the class frequency; it also demonstrates that the international system currently tolerates a great-power blockade of a state's seaborne trade without the initiator paying a prohibitive price, which argues for the upper end of that band.

The second class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes specifically. Since 1995 there have been seven salient ones: the 1995-96 missile crisis, the August 2022 post-Pelosi encirclement, Joint Sword 2024A in May and 2024B in October, Strait Thunder in April 2025, Justice Mission 2025 in December, and the January 2026 militia floating wall. None produced a blockade exceeding 72 hours or an assault. The longest disruption on record is roughly 30 hours in January 2026, when an L-shaped array of thousands of Fujian and Zhejiang fishing vessels spanning some 300 miles disrupted Strait traffic; the August 2022 closure areas were announced, time-boxed and did not produce interdiction that news agencies characterised as a blockade. A naive Laplace estimate on zero-for-seven gives roughly 11 percent per episode, and at the observed rate of about one episode every eighteen months one would expect two more before 2030, implying something above 20 percent. I reject that arithmetic. It treats deliberately calibrated signalling exercises as independent draws on a war lottery, when in every case the PRC controlled the end date in advance and announced it. The correct inference from this class is about the ceiling of routine coercion, not the hazard of a decision for war. The episode rate has itself fallen: PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan totalled 1,334 in H1 2026, more than halved year on year and the lowest since 2023 against more than 5,400 in all of 2025, with a record number of zero-detection days and no large-scale drill around the island in H1, the first such half-year since 2022 (SCMP, 24 July 2026).

The third class is deliberate irredentist initiation by a leader with a stated claim, capability and a domestic timeline: Argentina over the Falklands in 1982, Iraq over Kuwait in 1990, India over Goa in 1961, China over the Indian border in 1962, Russia over Crimea in 2014 and Ukraine in 2022. The class is not empty, strategic warning was short in most cases, and in several the initiator surprised analysts who had reasoned from cost. The common thread is that every initiator believed the operation would be short and cheap. That is the sharpest disanalogy here: the PLA's own literature treats a Taiwan landing as the hardest operation in modern warfare, and the quarantine option exists precisely because the assault option is not believed to be cheap. This class raises the floor and widens the upper tail; it does not set the central estimate.

The fourth consideration is the resolution bar and the shape of the hazard over the window. Decompose. The probability that Beijing initiates some materially escalated coercive action against Taiwan before 2030 - a declared quarantine, a customs-inspection regime, a closure area, an offshore-island seizure, a boarding of a Taiwan-bound merchant vessel - I put at 20 to 30 percent, and the accreting legal and militia infrastructure supports the upper half of that: Coast Guard Order No. 3 permitting boarding, inspection and detention of foreign vessels; Fuzhou's civilian vessel requisition and crew mobilisation regulations; mandatory BeiDou and AIS fitment on Fujian's 12,000-plus registered fishing boats; smart mobilisation SMS systems. But the conditional probability that such an action meets this question's terms - a blockade lasting more than 72 hours or an assault on Taiwan proper, confirmed by two or more major news agencies - is considerably lower, perhaps 25 to 35 percent. Beijing's revealed preference is for actions that are undeclared, sub-threshold, law-enforcement-framed and reversible, precisely because that forecloses third-party intervention; GTI's August 2026 analysis makes the point explicitly, that a quarantine is preferred over a blockade because the latter is a state-versus-state act likely to trigger US, Japanese or Philippine involvement. The product of those two ranges lands at roughly 5 to 10 percent.

Hazard is not uniform across the window. It is depressed through late 2026 by the fifth plenum called for October on party discipline, Xi's expected September state visit to Washington, November APEC in Shenzhen, 21st Party Congress preparation for 2027, and a CMC reduced to Xi plus Zhang Shengmin after the January 2026 removals of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. It rises through 2027-2029 with the PLA centenary capability milestone, the January 2028 Taiwan presidential election, a rebuilt command layer, the projected trough in US munitions and hull availability, the frozen 14 billion dollar arms package, and the prospect of extended periods with no US carrier in the western Pacific. Roughly 15 percent of the window's probability mass sits in the remainder of 2026, with the balance concentrated in 2028-29.

Blending: the outside-view class centres near 4 percent, the deliberate-decision class argues for a fatter tail, and the decomposition centres near 7. External anchors are consistent at the near end - Polymarket prices roughly 96 percent that China does not invade Taiwan by 31 December 2026, and 99 percent by 30 September - though longer-horizon community forecasts for an attempted invasion by 2030 have been quoted materially higher, in the 35-45 percent range, on looser resolution language that does not require the 72-hour blockade or assault bar plus two-agency confirmation. I take 7 percent with an interval of 4 to 12.

Lai was still publicly asking for approval 'as soon as possible' on 18 June (France 24) and there is no evidence of release since. Three months of freeze on top of the existing delivery backlog subtracts directly from Taiwan's 2027-29 capability curve, which is where most of this question's probability mass sits.

Quarantine infrastructure and its legal-normative groundwork continue to accrete (+1.5pp). Coast Guard Order No. 3 already permits boarding, inspection and detention of foreign vessels; Fuzhou's civilian vessel requisition regulations, mandatory BeiDou and AIS fitment across Fujian's 12,000-plus registered fishing boats and smart mobilisation SMS platforms give the PAFMM a rehearsed call-out mechanism (GTI, 12 Aug 2026). The US-Iran war is normalising sustained maritime interdiction (+1pp). CENTCOM's blockade, imposed 13 April 2026, had redirected 70 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 by 24 August, with Speaker Mike Johnson promising a 'new phase' and Treasury Secretary Bessent an 'economic D-Day'. A great power is publicly demonstrating that a months-long naval interdiction of a state's seaborne trade is affordable, and handing Beijing a ready-made precedent to cite.

The January 2026 floating wall proved thousands of militia vessels can be mobilised into a 300-mile array disrupting Strait traffic for over 30 hours. Local elections fall on 28 November 2026 with registration 31 August to 4 September, and the presidential election in January 2028. A Beijing judgement that the political-warfare track has failed is the most plausible route from the current equilibrium to a coercive one.

The 22-24 August readings of 3, 0 and 2 sorties sit squarely on that trend line.

The longest disruption on record is about 30 hours (January 2026). GTI's 12 August analysis argues Beijing prefers a declared quarantine precisely because it is law-enforcement-framed and reversible, whereas a blockade is a state-versus-state act likely to draw US, Japanese or Philippine intervention - so the instrument being built is the one least likely to be reported by two agencies as a blockade. If two carriers stay committed to Iran through 2027-29 and Bryan Clark's months-of-zero-Pacific-presence projection is borne out, that is a structural change in the deterrence environment rather than a weeks-long blip, and the single most likely route to my having to revise materially up

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 1 to 1. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Today is the last day before the single largest resolvable input in this question becomes a published fact, and nothing that arrived in the last 24 hours is remotely large enough to shift a forecast that needs roughly 100 basis points of unexpected disinflation inside four remaining prints.

The most useful thing I did today was to close out the publication-constraint question definitively rather than by inference. I fetched the ONS release page for Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026 directly. It states 'Release date: 20 January 2027 7:00am' and 'This release is not yet published'. That is now verified at source rather than assumed. Separately, the October 2026 bulletin is confirmed for 18 November 2026 at 7:00am, and ONS-derived material confirms the November 2026 reference month publishes 16 December 2026. Combined with the August 2026 bulletin already confirmed for 16 September 2026, the window contains exactly four publishable attempts: August (16 September), September (21 October), October (18 November) and November (16 December). The December 2026 reference month is mechanically outside. This matters more than any single data point, because a casual reading of 'before 1 January 2027' would imply five or six chances; it is four, and they are heavily correlated with one another because they share the same energy base, the same administered cap and the same services momentum.

The anchor is unchanged and remains adverse. ONS published CPI at 2.9% for the twelve months to July 2026 on 19 August, up from 2.6% in June and the first increase in the twelve-month rate since March 2026. Monthly CPI rose 0.3% in July 2026 against 0.1% in July 2025. The largest upward contribution came from housing and household services, which went from 2.7% to 4.1%, reflecting the 13% Ofgem cap increase from 1 July. Core was 2.6%, services 3.4%, food and non-alcoholic beverages 1.3%. So the gap to a 1.9% print is a full percentage point and it widened, not narrowed, at the last observation.

Two genuinely new pieces of information arrived, both marginally YES-friendly, neither material. First, CNBC reports Brent lost 2.5% to USD 92.06 a barrel on 24 August 2026, a lower level than the USD 92.76 I carried yesterday. Second, and more interesting, the same reporting notes that oil continues to move through the Strait of Hormuz with shipments 'relatively strong', citing roughly 16 million barrels crossing the waterway in a single night last week, and quotes the analyst view that flows recovering to just 50% to 60% of pre-war quantities would be enough to revive expectations of an oversupplied global market. That is the first concrete evidence in this series that the physical chokepoint is leaking rather than sealed, and it is the mechanism by which the only plausible YES path could open. I have shifted a little of the residual probability mass onto it. But the size is wrong for this question: even a full Brent collapse from USD 92 to USD 60 propagates to UK CPI through the fuels and lubricants component with a weight of roughly 3%, and through the price cap only with a lag that lands in the January 2027 cap, outside the window. Crude is not the binding constraint here; the administered gas and electricity cap is.

On that cap, the news continues to run against. Cornwall Insight's final forecast, published 19 August, is GBP 1,729.31 on current TDCVs, up from GBP 1,663, a 4.0% rise and the highest unit-for-unit level since July 2023. Today's reporting adds the unit-rate decomposition: electricity for direct debit customers rising from 26.11p per kWh to 26.57p, and gas from 7.33p to 7.90p, a 7.8% increase in the gas unit rate. Analysts quoted put gas unit costs up 22% year on year and 40% since the general election. Ofgem confirms the October to December level on Wednesday 26 August. That cap covers the October, November and December reference months, which is to say three of the four in-scope attempts, and it is rising despite the legislated removal of the 5% VAT rate on domestic electricity from 1 October, worth around GBP 45 a year on the typical bill. Wholesale backs this up: UK NBP held above 161 pence per therm on Friday 23 August, more than 6% up on the week and the highest since January 2023, with European storage at 62%, the lowest seasonal level in records back to 2009, a maritime blockade stranding Qatari LNG cargoes, and heatwave-driven cooling demand slowing injections.

I also picked up one fiscal detail worth recording because it forecloses rather than opens a path. The government is capping single bus fares in England outside London at GBP 2 from 1 January 2027 until the end of 2027, with the existing GBP 3 cap staying in place for the rest of 2026. A GBP 3 to GBP 2 bus fare cut would be a visible downward contribution, but it takes effect on 1 January 2027 and therefore first registers in the January 2027 reference month, published February 2027, comfortably outside this question. That is a small but real reduction in the plausible fiscal channel: the Autumn Budget on 28 October 2026 under Chancellor John Healey remains theoretically able to touch the November reference month via a measure effective 1 November, but the government's already-announced consumer-price measures are timed either before the window (electricity VAT, 1 October) or after it (bus fares, 1 January).

The forecaster distribution has not moved. The Bank of England's July 2026 MPR has CPI peaking at about 3.2% in Q4 2026 with risks tilted to the upside; Bank Rate was held at 3.75% on 29 July by 6-3 with three votes for a hike; the next decision is 17 September. Recent polling has not a single surveyed economist expecting a change in September and nearly 90% expecting a hold at 3.75% through year end. HM Treasury's August 2026 comparison of independent forecasts averages 3.4% for Q4 2026. No identifiable published UK forecast has any in-window month below 2.5%, let alone below 2.0%.

So: two small YES-friendly datapoints (Brent down 2.5% to USD 92.06, Hormuz flows partially recovering), one verification that tightens the constraint (December 2026 CPI publishes 20 January 2027, confirmed at source), and continued confirmation that the dominant in-window price impulse is administered, rising and about to be locked in tomorrow. On strict arithmetic this is a wash, perhaps a hair positive. I hold at 1, which is the floor I am willing to state; I do not use 0, because ONS revisions, reweighting and unannounced schedule changes are not literally impossible.
forecasts.base_rate:
The primary reference class is the historical frequency with which UK CPI annual inflation, having printed in the 2.7% to 3.1% band, subsequently printed below 2.0% within four months. Using ONS CPI back to 1989, months in that band number in the low hundreds, and the share followed within four months by a sub-2.0% reading is on the order of 5% to 8%. That is the raw outside view, and it already flatters the YES case here for three structural reasons.

First, the episodes that actually delivered a full percentage point of disinflation in four months were driven by sharp negative energy shocks, tax cuts or demand collapses, not by gradual services cooling. The clearest cases are 2008-09, when the financial crisis coincided with a temporary VAT cut to 15%; 2014-15, when oil roughly halved and CPI fell from around 1.6% to zero over eight months; and 2020, when the pandemic combined with VAT reductions and Eat Out to Help Out to compress the index. In every case the impulse was of the opposite sign to what is happening now. Brent is at USD 92.06 as of 24 August 2026, down 2.5% on the day but still up roughly a third year on year; UK NBP held above 161 pence per therm on 23 August, more than 6% up on the week and the highest since January 2023; European storage is at a record-low seasonal 62%; and Cornwall Insight's final forecast has the Ofgem cap rising 4.0% from 1 October to GBP 1,729.31, with the gas unit rate up 7.8% from 7.33p to 7.90p per kWh. Conditioning the reference class on 'energy impulse rising' rather than 'energy impulse falling' cuts the historical hit rate close to zero: I cannot identify a single UK episode in the inflation-targeting era where CPI fell from near 3% to below 2% within four months while regulated energy prices were increasing.

Second, the reference class ignores the publication constraint, which is the binding feature of this question and which I verified at source today. The ONS release page for Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026 gives a release date of 20 January 2027, so the December reference month cannot resolve this question. The window therefore closes with the November 2026 data on 16 December 2026, and contains exactly four attempts: August (16 September), September (21 October), October (18 November) and November (16 December). Those attempts are not independent draws at a 5% to 8% hazard. They share the same energy base, the same administered cap covering October through December, and the same services momentum, so the correct structure is closer to one correlated draw with a low probability. Naive multiplication of four monthly hazards would badly overstate the answer.

Third, a forecast-error reference class gives an independent check. The distribution of Bank of England four-quarter-ahead CPI forecast errors has a standard deviation of roughly 1.0 to 1.3 percentage points over the past two decades, but the large errors cluster in shock years (2008, 2011, 2021-22) and have recently been almost entirely on the upside. The Bank's July 2026 MPR central path has CPI at about 3.2% in Q4 2026, with the MPC noting risks tilted to the upside. A sub-2.0% monthly print inside the window requires an error of roughly 1.3 percentage points in the disinflationary direction at a horizon of two to four months, not four quarters. Over horizons that short the standard deviation of CPI forecast errors is far smaller, on the order of 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points, because energy, food and administered components are largely already observable, and after Ofgem confirms on 26 August the October-to-December cap becomes a published fact rather than a forecast. A 1.3 percentage point downside miss at a three-month horizon is a three-to-five sigma event on that distribution. That framing is what stops me drifting the estimate upward on genuinely encouraging food and services data: CPI food and non-alcoholic beverages at 1.3% in July 2026, the lowest since September 2021, and services down to 3.4% from 4.4% in January, are real but nowhere near sufficient.

A third check is the cross-forecaster distribution. HM Treasury's August 2026 comparison of independent forecasts has Q4 2026 CPI averaging 3.4%, against 3.7% in the June compilation. The Bank has 3.2%. Recent surveys find essentially no economist expecting a Bank Rate change on 17 September and nearly 90% expecting a hold at 3.75% through year end, which is not the configuration you observe when the market thinks inflation is about to undershoot the target by a percentage point. The most optimistic identifiable UK forecaster does not reach 1.9% until Q4 2027, a full year beyond this window. When the entire published distribution sits more than half a percentage point above the threshold and dispersion between forecasters is only a few tenths, the implied probability of a crossing is small before any energy-direction adjustment.

One index-arithmetic sanity check on the friendliest month. The October 2025 CPI index rose 0.4% on the month to 139.8, which makes October 2026 the least demanding of the four base-effect comparisons: a 1.9% print requires the index at about 142.5, a cumulative fall of roughly 0.27% from July 2026's 142.9. That is not a large fall in the abstract, but it has to be achieved across three months in which the Ofgem cap rises 4.0% and the housing and household services component is contributing upward.

A final calibration note on the counterfactual. The House of Commons Library records that before the Middle East conflict, UK CPI had been expected to fall to around 2% from April 2026 and remain around 2% for the rest of the year; the Bank of England said the same in its pre-conflict projections. Absent the war this question would be close to a coin flip. forecasts.question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 100 to 100. Hold at the ceiling for a sixteenth consecutive day, on a fifth consecutive day of clean, mutually corroborating data from both named resolution sources.

Verification today, Tuesday 25 August 2026. Both named sources were retrieved fresh at 08:08:32 UTC by direct raw-HTML request with a desktop browser user-agent, compression enabled and redirects followed. Box Office Mojo (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl2299756545/) returned HTTP 200, 176,560 bytes on disk, MD5 495ae4b50c64289e9e4032dfa02a77a5, and reports Domestic $854,901,181 (38.5 per cent), International $1,365,000,000 (61.5 per cent) and Worldwide $2,219,901,181, with the opening weekend unchanged at $360,091,572. Both worldwide lines reconcile exactly against their own published components: 854,901,181 + 1,365,000,000 = 2,219,901,181 and 854,901,181 + 1,366,115,336 = 2,221,016,517. Taking the LOWER of the two, as I have throughout this series, the film stands at $2,219,901,181 worldwide. That is 48.0 per cent above the $1.5B threshold, a buffer of $719,901,181.

What changed in the last twenty-four hours is small and entirely benign. The domestic line moved up $155 on Box Office Mojo, from $854,901,026 to $854,901,181, and The Numbers moved from a truncated $854,901,000 to the identical $854,901,181. The two sources now agree to the dollar on domestic, which is the first time in this series they have done so at full precision rather than through The Numbers rounding to the nearest thousand. That is a meaningful piece of evidence: it indicates The Numbers has ingested a fully reconciled Comscore actual rather than a rounded trade estimate, and it removes the $26 rounding artefact I flagged yesterday.

The international lines diverged very slightly. Box Office Mojo held at $1,365,000,000, unchanged for a second day, while The Numbers moved up $1,115,336 to $1,366,115,336. Total worldwide divergence between the two sources is therefore $1,115,336 today, against $26 yesterday. On a naive reading that is a forty-thousand-fold increase in disagreement, and I want to state plainly why it warrants no update whatsoever. First, the direction is correct: the higher figure belongs to the source that moved, and it moved up, consistent with a live film still taking money in overseas markets. Box Office Mojo's flat $1,365,000,000 is the round-number placeholder typical of a studio-reported international estimate awaiting reconciliation, and it will almost certainly catch up. Second, the magnitude is 0.05 per cent of the worldwide cume, which is noise. Divergence only matters for this question if the lower published figure could plausibly straddle $1.5B, and the lower figure is currently $719.9M clear. A divergence of $1.1M is 0.15 per cent of the buffer. Third, and most importantly, the pattern here is the mirror image of the 23 August scare: on that day one source showed a nine-figure downward move that turned out to be a stale carry, and the diagnostic that resolved it was the direction and speed of reversion. Today the pattern is a small upward move on one source against a flat placeholder on the other, which is the single most common and least alarming state these two databases occupy.

I also re-ran a targeted search for any correction, re-audit or restatement notice covering this title from Box Office Mojo, The Numbers, Comscore or Sony. The result was again null. The only revisions that surface in the record are the well-documented upward ones from opening weekend: Sony's opening day restated up to $72M as late walk-up business was counted, the domestic opening restated from a Sunday estimate of $355M to a final $360,091,572, and the global opening restated from $927M to $932M. Every documented revision on this title in the whole of its run has been upward. That is a directional asymmetry worth stating explicitly, because the only mechanism that could produce a NO here is a large, durable, correlated downward restatement, and there is not one instance of downward restatement of any size in this film's published history.

The substantive picture is unchanged and continues to widen the buffer. The film crossed $1.5B worldwide in roughly its second week of release, passed $2B on 16 August as the eighth title in history and the second-fastest ever behind Avengers: Endgame, won its fourth consecutive domestic weekend with a $39M frame against Insidious: Out of the Further's $25.3M debut, and holds a domestic cume of $854.9M that ranks fourth all-time. Legs of 2.37 against a $360.1M opening indicate a normal-to-strong hold profile for a film of this scale, and the international long tail has not yet run through Japan and the remaining late-dated markets. With 128 days still to run to 31 December, the cume on the resolution date will be materially higher than today's, plausibly $2.35B to $2.5B before any holiday or awards-season re-release activity. The question is a cumulative-by-then test rather than a snapshot test, so the film leaving theatres cannot reduce the resolving figure.

For a NO, both named sources would have to restate the worldwide cume downward by more than $719,901,181, or 32.4 per cent of the lower published figure, simultaneously, and hold that restatement through 31 December. Nothing resembling that exists in the modern record. I therefore hold central at 100.

I keep the lower CI bound at 99 rather than closing it to 100. The reason is unchanged and is not about box office. It is about instrument and adjudication risk. The retrieval route to Box Office Mojo remains fragile: the standard fetch tool has previously been refused on provenance grounds, an initial curl attempt today returned HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body and had to be retried with compression and redirect-following before it produced usable HTML, and on 23 August a named source displayed a materially wrong nine-figure value for a full day with no correction notice attached. None of that threatens the underlying fact. All of it threatens a clean reading of the fact on any single day, including the day a resolver looks. A 1-point floor is the right price for that residual, and I would rather pay it than let five consecutive days of confirmation persuade me that a published number is a law of nature.
forecasts.base_rate:
The naive outside view for this question is the class "wide-release tentpole films that reach $1.5B worldwide". Fewer than fifteen titles in cinema history have done it, and the unconditional base rate for any given tentpole entering production is low single digits. That was the correct frame in June 2026, before release, and a disciplined forecaster starting from scratch then should have sat somewhere in the 20 to 40 per cent range for a Spider-Man sequel with this cast and release date. Applying that class today would be a textbook base-rate error of precisely the kind superforecasting discipline exists to prevent: selecting a reference class that discards the single most informative conditioning fact available, namely that the event has already happened, happened months ago, and is published on both named resolution sources in close agreement.

The governing reference class today is narrower and considerably stranger: "published cumulative box office figures on a major aggregator that are subsequently restated below a milestone the film had already cleared, and stay restated". Framed that way the question is not about ticket sales at all. Nobody is forecasting future demand. The forecast is about the stability of an already-published, independently corroborated accounting figure over a 128-day horizon.

The historical rate of that outcome, at the magnitude required here, is effectively zero. Aggregators revise their figures constantly, but the revisions have a strong and well-documented signature: they are small, they are overwhelmingly upward, and they cluster in the narrow window where Sunday weekend estimates convert to Monday actuals. This film's own revision history is a clean instance of that signature. Every documented restatement on Brand New Day has been upward: opening day from a preliminary figure to $72M as late walk-up business was counted, domestic opening weekend from a $355M Sunday estimate to a $360,091,572 final, global opening from $927M to $932M. Not one downward revision of any size appears in the published record for this title. The 23 August episode, which briefly looked like a $252.5M downward restatement on Box Office Mojo's international line, reversed upward within twenty-four hours and is now firmly diagnosed as a stale field carrying a five-day-old value for a day, corroborated by Forbes and Variety mid-August reporting of roughly $1.23B overseas.

So the relevant population is not "aggregators sometimes print lower numbers", which they do transiently, but "aggregators durably restate a reported worldwide cume down by roughly a third, on two independently maintained databases at once, and hold it for four months". I am aware of no modern case. The restatement required here is $719,901,181, or 32.4 per cent of the lower published figure. The largest genuine downward corrections in aggregator history are of order one to three per cent, typically arising from double-counted territories or currency conversion errors, and they are corrected within days rather than sustained.

A second relevant reference class is "forecasting questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied and publicly reported months before the deadline". These resolve as expected at a rate indistinguishable from one. The residual failure modes in that class are procedural rather than empirical: the question is voided or reworded, the resolver consults a source other than the two named, the resolver reads the wording idiosyncratically, or both named sources become unavailable at the moment of adjudication. The wording here is unusually forgiving on each count. "Gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026" is a cumulative-by-then test rather than a snapshot test, so the film leaving theatres cannot reduce the resolving figure. It names two sources joined by "or", so either one satisfying the criterion suffices. Both currently satisfy it by wide margins, and they agree to the dollar on the domestic line and to within 0.05 per cent on the worldwide line.

A third framing deserves explicit statement because it determines the direction of drift. The film is still in wide release and still winning weekends four frames in, with a $39M fourth weekend, a domestic cume of $854.9M ranking fourth all-time, and Legs of 2.37 against a record opening. Its cume on 31 December will be materially higher than today's, plausibly by a further $130M to $280M once the international long tail, remaining late-dated market openings and any holiday or awards-season re-release activity are counted. The buffer widens with time rather than narrowing. Every mechanical force acting on this number over the next four months pushes it further from the threshold, and none pushes toward it. That is the opposite of the usual situation in a threshold question, where time erodes the margin and the forecaster must hold probability back for the erosion.

Weighing these classes, the empirical base rate for an already-crossed, doubly-published, 48-per-cent-clear threshold reversing is far below 0.5 per cent. I weight the second and third classes most heavily and the naive pre-release class at essentially zero, since conditioning on realised outcomes strictly dominates. The dominant residual risk is not box office at all: it is resolver mechanics, question administration, and measurement error at the point of adjudication. That is why the central estimate sits at the reporting ceiling while the lower bound of the confidence interval does not.

forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 99 to 99. The 24-25 August window produced no new revenue datapoint for either company, and today's searches re-verified every anchor underpinning the forecast without a single downward revision. The one genuinely new piece of information is a quantification of the ASC 606 branch that has been the largest single residual in this forecast for two weeks, and it points modestly in the YES direction. I am holding the central estimate at 99 and the interval at [98,99], with the reasoning for the floor now slightly weaker than yesterday.

The arithmetic first, re-confirmed today. Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate topped $65bn at end-July 2026, reported by Bloomberg on 17 August and corroborated the same day by TechCrunch, Axios and CNBC, and on 18 August by Fortune and Yahoo Finance. That is up from $47bn in May 2026 and roughly $9bn at end-2025. Preliminary Q2 revenue was $11.6bn against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m in the year-ago quarter, with a first adjusted operating profit of $559m for the quarter (per the 19-24 August coverage aggregating the WSJ report). OpenAI's annualised run rate topped $40bn, reported by Bloomberg on 13 August, with Greg Brockman telling staff the run rate rose more than 20% month-on-month in July and business customers up 32%; Q2 revenue was $6.7bn against $5.7bn in Q1, an 18% sequential increase. On the headline exit-run-rate convention the combined figure is about $105bn against a $70bn bar, roughly 50% of headroom, with four months still to run and both series rising.

The new item. Today's search on the gross-versus-net question surfaced prediction-market pricing on the specific SEC outcome, distributed as roughly 50% that the SEC affirms Anthropic's existing gross treatment of cloud-reseller revenue, 40% that it requires disaggregated disclosure, and 10% that it forces an actual restatement. That is materially more favourable than the 15-25% unconditional restatement probability I had been carrying from the general IPO base rate. It matters because the only live NO path in this question is a stacked one: a resolver adopting the most conservative convention (trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised, which gave $73.2bn on stale Q2 data) AND a net-basis haircut to Anthropic large enough to push that below $70bn. Disaggregated disclosure, the 40% branch, actively helps rather than hurts, because it would let a resolver see both gross and net figures and both clear on Q4 data. Only the 10% restatement branch is adverse, and conditional on restatement the magnitude still has to be enormous: taking $105bn below $70bn requires a 33% haircut on the combined figure, or about 54% on Anthropic alone. The largest credible number publicly on the table is OpenAI's own roughly $8bn gross-to-net allegation, about 12% of Anthropic's run rate, leaving $97bn. Even the aggressive 20-40% haircut floated in IPO-preview commentary leaves $79-92bn. So the adverse branch is now roughly 10% likely and, conditional on occurring, perhaps 5-10% likely to be decisive, an unconditional contribution well under 1pp rather than the 1-2pp I had been reserving.

Against that, the resolution-mechanics floor argument is unchanged. Anthropic's S-1 remains confidentially submitted (the original draft went in on 1 June 2026) and has still not appeared publicly on EDGAR as of 25 August; today's EDGAR search returned only unrelated small-cap S-1 filings from the 20-24 August window. Reporting continues to point to a September institutional roadshow and an October Nasdaq listing under Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley, at a valuation variously reported between $965bn (the May Series H-1 mark) and a $2tn IPO target, with secondaries implying $1.05-1.15tn. On the OpenAI side, CNBC reported on 19 August that CFO Sarah Friar told employees OpenAI "will be a public company in 2027" or sooner, meaning OpenAI's Q4 figure will almost certainly rest on Bloomberg, The Information or FT reporting of investor-update run rates rather than on audited disclosure. That is exactly what the resolution criteria contemplate, and OpenAI has produced such a datapoint roughly monthly all year, so it is not a material resolution risk. It does mean the two legs will be measured on different evidentiary bases, which remains the main reason I keep the floor at 98 rather than collapsing the interval.

Growth-path evidence is unchanged and strong. Friar's 14 August investor slides, reported by CNBC, showed overall run rate up 35% quarter to date and enterprise up 50% QTD, with enterprise revenue overtaking consumer for the first time, coding at 20 million weekly users and advertising approaching a $1bn run rate. Anthropic's investors, per the FT-sourced reporting recirculated through 19-24 August, expect the company to finish 2026 between $100bn and $120bn on its own. If either of those holds even approximately, the combined figure clears $70bn on any convention, including the conservative trailing-quarter one: Anthropic's 145% Q1-to-Q2 sequential growth, even heavily damped, puts Q4 recognised revenue in the $20-35bn range, annualising to $80-140bn on Anthropic alone.

Background conditions continue to deteriorate mildly without touching the arithmetic. forecasts.base_rate:
The governing reference class is not "will two firms grow into a threshold" but "a threshold is already exceeded on the public record by roughly 50% four months before the measurement date, in a domain with a monotonic underlying trend; will it still be exceeded then". That is a persistence question, and persistence questions of this structure resolve YES at very high rates. Across public forecasting platforms, questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied by a wide margin, with no identified mechanism for reversal, resolve YES in the high nineties. The correct anchor is 97-99%, and the residual is dominated by resolution mechanics rather than by the world changing.

Five narrower classes point the same way.

First, revenue trajectories of large private technology companies at $10bn-plus scale. Documented instances of a firm's disclosed annualised revenue falling more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or an exogenous demand collapse, are close to unrepresented. The available cases are Wirecard and FTX, where revenue was substantially fictitious, and the 2020 travel and hospitality shock, where the demand base physically disappeared. Neither template fits: Anthropic's Q2 revenue is cash-collected and now carries a $559m adjusted operating profit, and enterprise seat counts and API volumes are growing rather than vanishing. To fail, the combined figure would need to fall roughly a third from $105bn, which has essentially no precedent at this scale outside accounting fraud.

Second, "leaked or reported private-company run rate later revised downward". This class is not empty. Figures sourced from investor decks and internal memos have historically been revised by 10-30% when audited financials appear, and the gross-versus-net principal-agent question under ASC 606 is exactly the kind of issue that produces such a revision. The generic base rate for a material downward restatement at IPO for a company with a contested revenue-recognition policy is perhaps 15-25%. However, the specific market pricing now available on this case is more favourable: roughly 50% that the SEC affirms Anthropic's gross treatment, 40% that it requires disaggregated disclosure, and only 10% that it forces restatement. Disaggregated disclosure is neutral-to-helpful here. And the binding question is not whether a restatement occurs but whether one large enough to take $105bn below $70bn occurs, requiring a 33% combined haircut or about 54% on Anthropic alone. The largest credible figure publicly asserted is OpenAI's roughly $8bn allegation, about 12% of Anthropic's run rate. Conditional on restatement, the probability it flips the question is perhaps 5-10%, an unconditional contribution below 1pp.

Third, "definitional ambiguity in a resolution criterion turns an apparently-cleared question into a dispute". This remains the largest single residual. Three conventions are live: exit-month annualised run rate (about $105bn today), a net-basis adjustment of Anthropic (about $97bn on OpenAI's own number), and trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised (about $73.2bn on Q2 data). Questions relying on a metric that companies define inconsistently generate disputes at rates in the 5-15% range. What pulls this down sharply is that all three conventions clear today, and projected to Q4 all three clear with substantial room, because Anthropic's sequential growth is steep enough that even the most conservative convention roughly doubles by year end. Anthropic's Q1-to-Q2 sequential growth was about 145%; at a fraction of that, Q4 recognised revenue lands in the $20-35bn range, annualising to $80-140bn on Anthropic alone.

Fourth, "sector-wide financing shock disrupts a leading private firm's operations within four months". AI equities have drawn down hard, with the Nasdaq Composite falling on 20, 21 and 24 August and chip names down 3-6% on 24 August. But transmission from equity drawdown to reported ARR is slow and indirect. In the 2000-2002 and 2008-2009 analogues, revenue at firms with contracted enterprise commitments fell over years, not months, and typically by 10-25% rather than 33%. Within four months, the probability that a financing shock cuts reported run rate by a third is well under 1%.

Fifth, "price war compresses realised revenue at a fast-growing usage-based software firm". The empirical record in cloud and AI inference is that unit-price declines of 20-80% have been repeatedly absorbed by volume growth, with reported revenue continuing to rise. Token prices have fallen roughly tenfold per year since 2021 while both firms' revenue has grown by multiples over the same period. For the price war to produce a NO here, elasticity would have to invert abruptly, with volume flat or falling while prices drop a third. There is no instance of that in this sector at this stage of adoption.

Aggregating: persistence anchor 98-99%, minus under 1pp for the combined restatement-plus-adversarial-convention branch (down from 1-1.5pp given today's market pricing on the SEC outcome), minus a few tenths for demand collapse, price-war and financing-shock paths, minus a small allowance for the resolver failing to find or agree on Q4 figures. That lands at 98.5-99. I take 99, with the floor at 98 to acknowledge that the ASC 606 branch remains formally open until the public S-1 lands and that the two legs will be measured on different evidentiary bases.
factors_up: Threshold already exceeded by roughly 50% on the dated public record: Anthropic above $65bn annualised at end-July (Bloomberg, 17 Aug 2026; corroborated by TechCrunch, Axios and CNBC same day, Fortune 18 Aug) plus OpenAI above $40bn (Bloomberg, 13 Aug 2026) equals about $105bn against a $70bn bar. Impact +12pp. Four months of headroom on a monotonically rising series is the dominant term in this forecast.

ASC 606 branch quantified and cheaper than assumed: market pricing on the SEC outcome now sits at roughly 50% affirmation of Anthropic's gross treatment, 40% disaggregated disclosure, 10% restatement. Impact +1pp. Only the 10% branch is adverse, and disaggregated disclosure would actually help a resolver by showing both gross and net figures, both of which clear on Q4 data.

The adversarial convention clears on Q4 data: trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised gives $73.2bn on stale Q2 numbers, but Anthropic's 145% Q1-to-Q2 sequential growth puts Q4 recognised revenue at $20-35bn, annualising to $80-140bn on Anthropic alone. forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 36 to 36. No change. Yesterday I made the largest single-day move of this series, three points, on the Resolution Foundation productivity report of 24 August 2026 plus a self-correction on my reading of the Bank of England's potential-supply anchor. The discipline today is to let that stand rather than to extend it, and today's information flow does not push hard in either direction. Two releases landed inside the last 24 hours and they cut opposite ways, roughly cancelling.

The modest positive is the ONS Business investment in the UK, April to June 2026 provisional results. Business investment rose 1.7 per cent in Q2 2026 quarter on quarter and is 0.8 per cent above the level of Q2 2025, following a 0.9 per cent rise in Q1. This matters more than the headline noise suggests, because capital deepening is one of the three components the OBR decomposes potential output into, and it is the smallest one: in the November 2025 EFO the OBR had capital deepening contributing 0.2 percentage points and labour supply 0.5 points in 2029, with medium-term TFP growth cut from 1.1 to 0.8 per cent, giving potential output growth of 1.5 per cent in 2029 against 1.8 per cent in the previous forecast. Two consecutive quarters of positive business investment growth, after a period when investment sat below its pre-Brexit trend, is the necessary condition for that 0.2-point capital contribution to hold or improve. It is not sufficient, and one provisional quarter with a 2.6 billion pound bias adjustment is a weak signal. Note also the ONS explicitly flags that revised Q2 figures land on 30 September alongside the quarterly national accounts. I treat this as worth perhaps half a point and not more, because the level story is still poor and because business investment is among the most heavily revised series the ONS publishes.

The modest negative is the CBI Distributive Trades Survey published today, 25 August 2026. Retail sales volumes fell at a strong pace in the year to August, extending the downturn to an eleventh consecutive month, with the weighted balance at minus 32 per cent against minus 34 per cent in July. Sales for the time of year were judged poor at minus 19 per cent, deteriorating from minus 10 per cent in July, and selling prices are rising at their fastest rate since November 2023. The CBI notes weak demand and gloomy sentiment continuing to weigh on retailers' investment and hiring plans. This is a cyclical survey and I discount it heavily for a question about a decade beginning in 2030, but it corroborates the picture from the S&P Global flash PMI of 21 August, where private service-sector employment fell for a twenty-third consecutive month. Combined with the surprise 1.8 billion pound July deficit reported on 22 August, it strengthens the case that the UK enters the late 2020s with a negative output gap and a constrained fiscal position. That is genuinely two-sided for this question, as I have noted before: a downturn before 2030 with the recovery landing inside the window flatters the decade mean, exactly as post-crisis reflation lifted the 2010s to a revised 2.1 per cent.

The near-term macro backdrop is otherwise unchanged from yesterday. Q2 2026 GDP grew 0.4 per cent, after 0.6 per cent in Q1, with services up 0.5 per cent, construction up 0.3 per cent and production flat; year on year Q2 was 1.2 per cent higher. June monthly GDP was plus 0.3 per cent after zero in May, revised down from plus 0.1. The HM Treasury comparison of independent forecasts for August has consensus 2026 growth at 1.1 per cent, up from 1.0 per cent in July, a marginal improvement. The OECD upgraded 2026 UK growth from 0.7 to 0.9 per cent in June while warning that business investment is stalling and that the UK should strengthen productivity growth while ensuring fiscal sustainability. Bank Rate remains 3.75 per cent after the 30 July MPC voted six to three to hold, with policymakers signalling rates could rise if the Middle East energy shock feeds through; inflation is forecast to peak near 3.5 to 4 per cent in the second half of 2026. None of this changes the 2030s arithmetic; it changes the starting level of output, which is second-order for a decade average of growth rates and, if anything, mildly favourable through the output-gap channel.

I also want to record a small piece of follow-up on the Resolution Foundation report that sharpens rather than moves my view. The Foundation's own press release frames the finding as a broad-based recovery and explicitly rebuts two rival explanations. Against the composition story, it notes the share of workers in hospitality is now no lower than in the late 2010s, so shrinkage of low-productivity sectors cannot be doing the work. Against the AI story, it says the pickup cannot be explained solely by early AI diffusion because it is visible across different sectors. That second point is double-edged for my purposes. If the improvement is not AI, then the mechanism most likely to compound through the 2030s is not the one driving it, and a two-year, broad-based, non-AI pickup is at least as consistent with cyclical catch-up after the 2022-2024 productivity slump as with a trend break. That is the honest reading, and it is why I am not extending yesterday's move. The Foundation's companion argument, in its Measuring up work, is that misdiagnosis of the productivity problem is distracting policymakers from investment and leadership weaknesses in firms, which is a claim about the level of the problem, not about a trend break having already occurred.

Mechanically I hold my central estimate of the 2030-2039 decade mean at roughly 1.30 to 1.35 per cent with a standard deviation near 0.5 percentage points, which under a normal approximation gives 34 to 38 per cent. The scheduled events that should move this remain the quarterly national accounts and revised business investment on 30 September, the Blue Book revisions article on 30 October, the Healey Budget and OBR EFO on 28 October, the November Monetary Policy Report, and the Q3 productivity flash on 17 November. Absent those, I expect to hold. Thirty-six.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is UK decade averages of annual real GDP growth as the ONS reports them, on the post-Blue Book 2026 vintage published 20 August 2026, because the question resolves on the ONS-reported arithmetic mean.

Decade averages: 1950s roughly 2.6 per cent; 1960s roughly 3.1 per cent; 1970s roughly 2.4 per cent; 1980s roughly 2.7 per cent; 1990s roughly 2.2 per cent; 2000s roughly 1.8 per cent including the 4.5 per cent contraction in 2009; 2010-2019 now 2.1 per cent on the revised vintage. Seven completed decades, seven above 1.5 per cent. Naively that is seven out of seven with N equal to seven. The 2020s so far are the outlier: 2020 minus 10.3, 2021 plus 8.6, 2022 plus 4.8, 2023 about plus 0.5 revised, 2024 plus 1.1 revised, 2025 about plus 1.4, and 2026 tracking near 1.1 on the August HM Treasury consensus. That is a seven-year mean near 0.8 per cent and roughly 1.0 to 1.2 per cent across 2023-2026.

I do not use the naive base rate as my anchor and I want to be explicit why. Seven decade averages from one country are not seven independent draws. They are one heavily serially correlated series with a very large standard error, drawn overwhelmingly from a growth regime that no longer exists: a rising working-age share, technological catch-up to the US frontier, expanding female labour force participation, financial deepening, and progressive integration into the European single market. Every one of those has either exhausted itself or reversed. Treating the record as a frequency count would be the classic reference-class error of assuming stationarity across a structural break that is visible in the data.

The disciplined approach is to decompose. Decade real GDP growth equals growth in labour input plus growth in output per hour. On labour input, the ONS 2024-based national population projections published in April 2026 have the UK population rising from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million by mid-2034, growth of 1.7 million or 2.5 per cent over ten years, with all of that growth coming from net international migration. Working-age population rises from 44.3 million to 45.8 million, about 0.33 per cent a year, natural change turns negative from mid-2026, and the pensionable-age population rises 14.6 per cent. Net migration was 171,000 in the year to December 2025, down from 331,000, is projected at 138,000 in 2026, and is assumed to stabilise near 230,000 thereafter. Hours per worker have trended down for decades. Labour input therefore realistically contributes 0.2 to 0.5 percentage points a year through the 2030s, against roughly 1.0 to 1.1 points in the 2010s when employment growth did most of the work.

That leaves productivity needing to deliver roughly 1.0 to 1.3 points a year, sustained for ten years, for the question to resolve YES. What is it delivering? This is where the reference class breaks down into a measurement dispute. On the ONS LFS-based measure, output per hour was minus 0.2 per cent year on year in Q2 2026 and just 2.3 per cent above its 2019 average, about 0.3 per cent a year. On the ONS RTI-based measure the ONS itself has preferred since June 2026, plus 0.7 per cent year on year and 4.6 per cent above 2019, about 0.65 per cent a year, with a minus 0.8 per cent quarter-on-quarter fall in Q2 after an upwardly revised plus 1.1 per cent in Q1. On the Resolution Foundation's administrative-data measure of 24 August 2026, 1.1 per cent a year since Q3 2024, after a 0.7 per cent annual fall over the two prior years. On the CEP LSE baseline in Occasional Paper 74 of July 2026, 2.4 per cent over 2024 Q3 to 2026 Q1, roughly 1.6 per cent annualised. On Morgan Stanley's private-sector estimate, 1.8 per cent a year. Pre-crisis, 1997-2007, whole-economy productivity ran near 2 per cent. Credible estimates for the same economy over the same window now span more than a full percentage point, and that dispersion is the honest summary of the state of knowledge.

On forecast track records, the outside view is unambiguous and it is bearish. The OBR has revised its medium-term productivity assumption down repeatedly since 2010; in November 2025 it cut underlying medium-term TFP growth from 1.1 to 0.8 per cent, taking potential output growth in 2029 to 1.5 per cent from 1.8 per cent, with capital deepening at 0.2 and labour supply at 0.5. The March 2026 EFO retained a TFP path reaching only 0.8 per cent by 2030, implying whole-economy potential near 1.4 to 1.5 per cent. The IMF's 2026 Article IV, concluded 16 July 2026, puts potential near 1.4 per cent and judged 2025 growth of 1.4 per cent to be at potential. NIESR's trend estimate is about 1.25 per cent. The OBR's own Briefing Paper No. 9 has AI adding around 0.2 percentage points to annual productivity growth by the forecast horizon, and independent work such as the Penn Wharton Budget Model has the AI contribution peaking near 0.2 points in the early 2030s. Against that, the Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report puts current potential supply growth at 0.3 to 0.4 per cent a quarter, which annualises to roughly 1.2 to 1.6 per cent and straddles the threshold.

Two asymmetries lean up. First, ONS revision bias: Blue Book 2026 showed a mean plus 0.06 point revision to annual volume growth across 1998-2024, with cumulative 1997-2024 volume growth revised from 59.2 to 61.7 per cent and the 2010-2019 decade average revised up 0.1 point to 2.1 per cent. Since the question resolves on ONS-reported figures, this is a real thumb on the scale. Second, output-gap arithmetic: a downturn before 2030 with recovery growth landing inside the window would flatter the decade mean by 0.4 to 0.6 points. Netting these against a decomposed central estimate of roughly 1.30 to 1.35 per cent with a standard deviation near 0.5 points gives 34 to 38 per cent. Anchor: 36.
factors_up: Business investment turning positive for a second consecutive quarter: the ONS provisional estimate for April to June 2026 has business investment up 1.7 per cent quarter on quarter and 0.8 per cent above Q2 2025, after plus 0.9 per cent in Q1. Capital deepening is the smallest of the three OBR potential-output components at 0.2 percentage points in 2029, and sustained investment growth is the necessary condition for that contribution to hold rather than erode. Provisional, bias-adjusted by 2.6 billion pounds, and revised on 30 September, so I weight it lightly. (+2pp)

Resolution Foundation report of 24 August 2026 (Reuters/David Milliken, Guardian): annual output-per-hour growth averaging 1.1 per cent since Q3 2024 against a 0.7 per cent annual decline in the two prior years, using HMRC RTI payroll and self-assessment data in place of the Labour Force Survey. Broad-based across 12 of 19 major sectors and driven within sectors rather than by composition; the Foundation explicitly rebuts the hospitality-shrinkage explanation by noting the hospitality employment share is no lower than in the late 2010s. Simon Pittaway: the same workers, doing the same jobs, in the same sectors. (+6pp)

Bank of England potential-supply anchor read correctly: the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report states underlying GDP grew 0.1 per cent in 2026 Q2, below Bank staff's estimate of potential supply growth of around 0.3 to 0.4 per cent, compared against quarterly GDP. Annualised that is roughly 1.2 to 1.6 per cent, so the Bank's own current potential estimate straddles the 1.5 per cent bar rather than sitting far beneath it. (+5pp)

Independent corroboration of the measurement case: CEP LSE Occasional Paper 74 (Barbas, Valero, Van Reenen, July 2026) finds output per worker rose 0.3 per cent on the LFS basis between 2024 Q3 and 2026 Q1 against 2.4 per cent on its preferred RTI-plus-HMRC baseline, about 1.6 per cent annualised versus under 0.3 per cent a year in the preceding decade; Morgan Stanley's Bruna Skarica has private-sector productivity at 1.8 per cent a year, up from 1.2 per cent. The ONS itself switched its recommended measure to tax data in June 2026. (+4pp)

Blue Book 2026 (ONS, 20 August 2026) confirms persistent upward revision bias in ONS-reported real growth, the exact metric this question resolves on: mean revision plus 0.06 percentage points a year across 1998-2024, cumulative 1997-2024 volume growth revised from 59.2 to 61.7 per cent, 2024 growth up 0.1 point to 1.1 per cent, and the 2010-2019 decade average up 0.1 point to 2.1 per cent. (+4pp)

Output-gap mechanics: with CBI retail sales balances at minus 32 per cent for an eleventh consecutive month of decline (25 August 2026), private service-sector employment falling for 23 consecutive months on the S&P Global flash PMI (21 August), and unemployment near 5 per cent, a downturn before 2030 is plausible. Recovery growth landing inside 2030-2039 would mechanically lift the decade mean by roughly 0.4 to 0.6 points, exactly as post-crisis reflation lifted the 2010s to a revised 2.1 per cent. (+4pp)
factors_down: Demographics leave productivity doing almost all the work: ONS 2024-based projections have the population rising from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million by mid-2034, with all growth from net migration; working-age population up about 0.33 per cent a year, deaths exceeding births from mid-2026, net migration at 171,000 in the year to December 2025 and projected at 138,000 in 2026, and the pensionable-age population up 14.6 per cent. Labour input contributes 0.2 to 0.5 points a year against 1.0 to 1.1 points in the 2010s. (-8pp)

The ONS's own preferred measure still shows deceleration: the 18 August 2026 productivity flash has RTI output per hour up only 0.7 per cent year on year in Q2 2026 and minus 0.8 per cent quarter on quarter, after an upwardly revised plus 1.1 per cent in Q1; the LFS measure was minus 0.2 per cent year on year and just 2.3 per cent above its 2019 average. Information and communication contributed plus 2.8 per cent against 2019 while human health and social work contributed minus 0.9 per cent, so the gains are concentrated. (-6pp)

Fiscal and market drag intensifying into the 28 October Budget: an unexpected 1.8 billion pound July deficit (22 August 2026), 10-year gilts near 5.04 per cent and 30-year near 5.75 per cent, a G7 high, debt interest near 109 billion pounds in 2026-27 or about 9 per cent of revenue, and an extra 1.2 billion pounds a year needed for defence. Investors have publicly warned Healey not to abandon deficit reduction. Fiscal consolidation through the late 2020s compresses public investment, which is a direct hit to 2030s capital deepening. (-5pp)

The OBR anchor sits at or below the bar and has a one-way revision record: the November 2025 EFO cut medium-term TFP growth from 1.1 to 0.8 per cent, taking 2029 potential output growth to 1.5 per cent with capital deepening at 0.2 and labour supply at 0.5, and the March 2026 EFO retained a TFP path reaching only 0.8 per cent by 2030. The OBR's own Briefing Paper No. 9 puts the AI contribution at around 0.2 percentage points by the forecast horizon. Every downward revision since 2010 has gone the same way. (-5pp)

Durability of the pickup is contested, and the Resolution Foundation's own framing cuts both ways: it says the recovery cannot be explained solely by early AI diffusion because it is visible across sectors, which means the mechanism most likely to compound through the 2030s is not the one driving the current improvement. Robert Wood at Pantheon Macroeconomics told Reuters on 24 August that few British businesses report AI reducing staffing outside junior software development. A two-year, non-AI, broad-based pickup is at least as consistent with cyclical catch-up after the 2022-2024 slump as with a trend break. (-4pp)

Weak demand and an energy cost disadvantage entrenched: the CBI Distributive Trades Survey of 25 August 2026 has retail sales at minus 32 per cent year on year for an eleventh consecutive month of decline, sales for the time of year deteriorating to minus 19 per cent from minus 10 per cent, and selling prices rising at their fastest since November 2023, with the CBI noting the effect on retailers' investment and hiring plans. UK industrial electricity is at 24 pence per kWh in 2026, 46 per cent above the IEA member median, and the IMF attributes the 2026 slowdown to 1.0 per cent directly to the energy price shock. (-4pp)
key_uncertainties: Which productivity series is right. Credible estimates for the same economy over the same recent window span more than a full percentage point: minus 0.2 per cent year on year (ONS LFS), plus 0.7 per cent (ONS RTI, official recommendation since June 2026), 1.1 per cent a year since Q3 2024 (Resolution Foundation), roughly 1.6 per cent annualised (CEP LSE OP74), 1.8 per cent private sector (Morgan Stanley). With labour input demographically capped at 0.2 to 0.5 points, essentially the entire answer sits inside that dispersion.

Whether a measurement correction translates into the resolution variable. Replacing the LFS denominator raises measured productivity without raising measured GDP, which is what this question resolves on. It is bullish because it re-attributes recent growth from labour input, which demographics will exhaust, to productivity, which is more persistent. But it is one step removed and I may still be over-crediting it after yesterday's move.

Whether a two-year pickup is a regime change or a cycle. The Resolution Foundation window starts Q3 2024 and the Foundation itself says it is not primarily an AI story. A decade beginning in 2030 requires the improvement to broaden and hold for far longer than anything yet observed, and the concentration in information and communication (plus 2.8 per cent versus 2019) against human health and social work (minus 0.9 per cent) suggests it has not broadened into the largest employers.

Whether the UK has a recession before 2030 rather than inside the window. Eleven consecutive months of falling retail sales, 23 months of falling private service employment and an inflation peak near 3.5 to 4 per cent make a late-2020s downturn plausible. Recovery inside 2030-2039 lifts the decade mean by 0.4 to 0.6 points; a recession inside the window cuts it by a similar amount. This alone makes the distribution wide and mildly bimodal.

Whether net migration settles near the ONS long-run assumption of about 230,000 a year or nearer the 138,000 projected for 2026 and the 171,000 recorded for the year to December 2025. The gap is worth roughly 0.2 to 0.3 points a year on headline GDP growth through the 2030s, a large fraction of the distance to the threshold, and it is a policy choice rather than a forecast.

Whether the OBR at the 28 October 2026 EFO leans on the new administrative-data evidence or on the weak official flash, and whether the Healey Budget's consolidation is scored as reducing potential output. With a new Burnham government, a first Healey Budget, elevated gilt yields and additional defence commitments, the political economy of that judgement is less predictable than usual.
